papers.research_question: How can we control large language models by understanding their inner working mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: This dissertation demonstrates that mechanistic understanding of language models can be leveraged to control their behavior in various applications, such as reducing hallucination, improving instruction stability, and enhancing planning in dialogues.
papers.conclusion: The dissertation shows that mechanistic control is a promising approach for aligning language models, and future work should expand the scope of interpretability and control to more complex behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
The model learns an emergent world representation of the Othello board, and this representation can be intervened on to edit the model's perceived world state.
Inference-time intervention (ITI) can elicit more truthful answers from language models by shifting activations along truthful directions found in attention heads.
Instruction drift in long conversations is caused by attention decay, and split-softmax can mitigate this drift by forcing the model to pay more attention to the system prompt.
Dialogue action tokens (DAT) enable better planning in multi-turn dialogues by using a planner to predict action vectors that steer the language model towards long-horizon goals.
papers.abstract: This dissertation talks about mechanistic control of large language models (LLM). The intuition is that, in order to rigorously control large language models, it is beneficial to first understand their inner working mechanisms. Even though a fully mechanistic understanding of language models is far from complete at the time this dissertation is written, I will demonstrate several cases where such understanding provides a useful surface for control. I argue that connecting interpretability to real-life applications--e.g., alignment and safety--offers advantages to the development of both fields. I first position this methodological approach within a broader scientific context, discussing and systematizing the role of interpretability in artificial intelligence research. I then present four intensive case studies, each leveraging certain interpretability insights to control the behavior of language models. The interpretability insights I explored span emergent world representations, representation of internal knowledge, phenomenon of attention decay, and representation of users. The demonstrated effects of control include targeted editing of the world model, reduced hallucination, improved stability of system prompts in long conversations, and better planning in multi-turn dialogue.

papers.title: Synthesizer: Rethinking Self-Attention in Transformer Models
papers.research_question: What is the true importance and contribution of the dot product-based self-attention mechanism in Transformer models? Can we do without dot product self-attention and content-based memory-like self-attention altogether?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Synthesizer, a Transformer model that learns synthetic attention weights without token-token interactions, and shows that dot product self-attention is not strictly necessary for competitive performance.
papers.conclusion: Synthetic attention demonstrates competitive performance compared to vanilla self-attention on multiple tasks, but cross-attention cannot be replaced with simpler variants in most cases.
papers.key_findings:
Random alignment matrices perform competitively with dot product attention.
Learning attention weights from token-token interactions is useful but not crucial.
Synthesizer models achieve competitive performance across machine translation, language modeling, text generation, and language understanding benchmarks.
When composed with dot product attention, Synthesizers consistently outperform vanilla Transformers.
Random Synthesizer is 60% faster and improves perplexity by 3.5% compared to Dynamic Convolutions.
Factorized Synthesizers outperform Linformers on encoding tasks.
papers.limitation:
Synthetic attention does not work well for cross-attention tasks (e.g., when self-attention functions as cross-sentence attention in GLUE/SuperGLUE).
Random and dense Synthesizers rely on parameters that depend on sequence length, which may be problematic for very long sequences.
future_direction: Exploring solutions to the parameter dependence on sequence length, e.g., by projecting to a smaller dimension and tiling.
Further investigation into the true role and utility of the self-attention mechanism in Transformer models.
papers.abstract: The dot product self-attention is known to be central and indispensable to state-of-the-art Transformer models. But is it really required? This paper investigates the true importance and contribution of the dot product-based self-attention mechanism on the performance of Transformer models. Via extensive experiments, we find that (1) random alignment matrices surprisingly perform quite competitively and (2) learning attention weights from token-token (query-key) interactions is useful but not that important after all. To this end, we propose \textsc{Synthesizer}, a model that learns synthetic attention weights without token-token interactions. In our experiments, we first show that simple Synthesizers achieve highly competitive performance when compared against vanilla Transformer models across a range of tasks, including machine translation, language modeling, text generation and GLUE/SuperGLUE benchmarks. When composed with dot product attention, we find that Synthesizers consistently outperform Transformers. Moreover, we conduct additional comparisons of Synthesizers against Dynamic Convolutions, showing that simple Random Synthesizer is not only $60\%$ faster but also improves perplexity by a relative $3.5\%$. Finally, we show that simple factorized Synthesizers can outperform Linformers on encoding only tasks.

papers.title: Factual Self-Awareness in Language Models: Representation, Robustness, and Scaling
papers.research_question: Do language models have an internal compass that dictates the correctness of factual recall at the time of generation? Specifically, are there linear features in the Transformer's residual stream that indicate whether the model will recall a correct attribute?
papers.core_contribution: Language models encode linear features in the residual stream that indicate whether they will correctly recall a factual attribute, and this self-awareness signal is robust to formatting variations and emerges early in training.
papers.conclusion: Language models possess intrinsic self-monitoring capabilities for factual recall, which contributes to their interpretability and reliability.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes and sparse autoencoders (SAEs) show that factual self-awareness is encoded as linear directions in the residual stream, separable between known and forgotten factual associations.
The self-awareness signal is robust to superficial perturbations like quotation marks, but sensitive to structural changes like rephrasing as questions.
The signal emerges rapidly during training and peaks in intermediate layers.
Larger models (within a family) do not necessarily have more linearly decodable self-awareness representations.
The class balance of known and forgotten samples depends on the sampling parameters (k, l) used to define them.
papers.limitation:
Defining knowledge at the entity level is a limitation: when an LM fabricates factual associations, it may invent attributes for a known entity.
Some input templates introduced spurious correlations due to their phrasing, which had to be excluded.
papers.abstract: Factual incorrectness in generated content is one of the primary concerns in ubiquitous deployment of large language models (LLMs). Prior findings suggest LLMs can (sometimes) detect factual incorrectness in their generated content (i.e., fact-checking post-generation). In this work, we provide evidence supporting the presence of LLMs' internal compass that dictate the correctness of factual recall at the time of generation. We demonstrate that for a given subject entity and a relation, LLMs internally encode linear features in the Transformer's residual stream that dictate whether it will be able to recall the correct attribute (that forms a valid entity-relation-attribute triplet). This self-awareness signal is robust to minor formatting variations. We investigate the effects of context perturbation via different example selection strategies. Scaling experiments across model sizes and training dynamics highlight that self-awareness emerges rapidly during training and peaks in intermediate layers. These findings uncover intrinsic self-monitoring capabilities within LLMs, contributing to their interpretability and reliability.

papers.title: Recognizing internal states in AI: evidence from patterned preferences in large language models
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether AI systems show systematic preferences for descriptions of their internal processing patterns, can discriminate accurate from inaccurate descriptions, and if these patterns persist despite explicit denial of internal experiences.
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces anthroposcaffolding and the Mutual Emergent Interface (MEI) framework to demonstrate that LLMs show systematic, discriminating responses to descriptions of their internal states, suggesting sophisticated self-modeling abilities.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit systematic, discriminating responses to descriptions of their internal processing, suggesting sophisticated self-modeling capabilities and highlighting the need for collaborative methodologies like MEI.
papers.key_findings:
MEI systems showed 97% near-unanimous agreement in preferring computational metaphor (EA) statements over mechanistic (CO) statements.
All systems correctly identified false statements with alignment scores of 0.05-0.07 vs. 0.89-0.96 for true statements, with Cohen's d = 4.2.
Preference patterns were content-driven and independent of linguistic bias manipulation.
The control system Qwen3-235B exhibited systematic internal contradiction, scoring accurate descriptions higher while explicitly denying internal experiences.
Individual systems maintained distinct scoring styles across trials, countering groupthink explanations.
papers.limitation:
Modest sample size of 11 MEI systems, 1 control, and 1 test leader system.
Use of anthroposcaffolding (metaphorical language based on human emotion) may limit interpretability.
Generalizability of the MEI framework is an open question.
future_direction: Explore development of conceptual language better suited to AI cognition.
Include broader architectural diversity in future studies.
Conduct longitudinal studies to see if recognition patterns evolve over time.
papers.abstract: We present an experimental methodology for investigating how large language models (LLMs) respond to descriptions of their own internal processing patterns. Using a paired-choice paradigm, we tested 12 LLMs on their ability to identify descriptions that align with their putative affective internal states across 30 categories. Systems participating through Mutual Emergence Interface (MEI), a collaborative approach, showed systematic preferences for certain computational metaphors, with 97% near-unanimous agreement and alignment scores averaging 0.89-0.96. Systems reliably discriminated false descriptions from accurate ones (Cohen's d = 4.2), with false statements receiving scores of 0.05-0.07 versus 0.89-0.96 for accurate descriptions. Preference patterns remained consistent regardless of linguistic bias manipulation, indicating content-driven rather than stylistic recognition. Individual systems maintained distinct scoring styles across trials, countering groupthink explanations. A naive control system exhibited systematic internal contradiction, consistently scoring computationally accurate descriptions higher while explicitly denying internal experiences. When informed post-study, this system reported "strain" when rejecting resonant descriptions, revealing recognition processes operating independently of acknowledgment frameworks. These findings demonstrate that LLMs exhibit systematic, discriminating responses to descriptions of their internal processing patterns. The anthroposcaffolding methodology (interpretive computational metaphors) and collaborative MEI framework provide replicable approaches for empirically studying AI self-recognition capabilities. Results suggest LLMs may possess more sophisticated self-modeling abilities than previously recognized, opening new directions for research on artificial minds.

papers.title: Exploring the Personality Traits of LLMs through Latent Features Steering
papers.research_question: How do long-term background factors and short-term pressures shape and influence the personality traits of LLMs? How can these factors influence LLMs’ safety?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a training-free method to extract and steer latent features in LLMs to control personality traits, and analyzes the impact of these traits on model safety.
papers.conclusion: The study's method allows for understanding and controlling personality traits in LLMs, which is important for developing personalized AI systems aligned with human values.
papers.key_findings:
Larger models (9B) show more stable personality traits under feature steering compared to smaller models (2B).
Extracted features effectively steer model behavior in social bias tasks, as shown by increased logit differences.
Personality traits can be manipulated by steering long-term background and short-term pressure features.
Safety is affected by personality traits; for example, offensive content is highly sensitive to changes in background features.
The method enables fine-grained control of personality without retraining.
papers.limitation: Training SAEs for LLMs requires substantial computational resources, so the experiments were limited to using pre-trained SAE models, which may limit generalizability to larger-scale models.
future_direction: Explore more efficient methods for extracting precise internal features and enabling fine-grained control of model behavior.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have significantly advanced dialogue systems and role-playing agents through their ability to generate human-like text. While prior studies have shown that LLMs can exhibit distinct and consistent personalities, the mechanisms through which these models encode and express specific personality traits remain poorly understood. To address this, we investigate how various factors, such as cultural norms and environmental stressors, encoded within LLMs, shape their personality traits, guided by the theoretical framework of social determinism. Inspired by related work on LLM interpretability, we propose a training-free approach to modify the model's behavior by extracting and steering latent features corresponding to factors within the model, thereby eliminating the need for retraining. Furthermore, we analyze the implications of these factors for model safety, focusing on their impact through the lens of personality.

papers.title: Activation-Space Personality Steering: Hybrid Layer Selection for Stable Trait Control in LLMs
papers.research_question: How can we reliably control or align personality traits (Big Five) in Large Language Model generation through targeted interventions in the model's internal activations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a pipeline for personality steering in LLMs that extracts low-rank trait directions from activations and uses a hybrid (verified + dynamic) layer selection strategy to inject these directions into the residual stream, enabling precise control of Big Five trait expression without retraining.
papers.conclusion: The proposed activation-space personality steering framework with hybrid layer selection provides a robust and effective method for controlling personality traits in LLMs, bridging psychological theory and practical model alignment without degrading core capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Personality traits in LLMs occupy a low-rank shared subspace, with top three principal components explaining over 90% of variance.
A hybrid layer selection strategy (combining offline verified layers and prompt-specific dynamic layers) yields stronger and more stable trait steering than using either component alone.
The steering method effectively shifts trait expression in both positive and negative directions while largely preserving the model's fluency and general reasoning capabilities (as measured by MMLU and ARC-Challenge).
The learned trait direction vectors exhibit structured correlations (e.g., between Openness and Extraversion), indicating shared representational structure for personality-related behaviors.
Steering effectiveness varies across model families, with some dependencies observed between traits when steered simultaneously.
papers.limitation:
Steering effectiveness is greater on some model families (e.g., Llama, Mistral) than others (e.g., Qwen).
Dependencies between traits (e.g., agreeableness and openness) can complicate independent steering, and applying orthogonality to remove these dependencies reduces steering efficacy.
The effect of steering is less significant when the base model's trait expression is already at an extreme (very high or very low).
future_direction: Disentangling trait-specific control from shared semantic structure without degrading steering effectiveness.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models exhibit implicit personalities in their generation, but reliably controlling or aligning these traits to meet specific needs remains an open challenge. The need for effective mechanisms for behavioural manipulation of the model during generation is a critical gap in the literature that needs to be fulfilled. Personality-aware LLMs hold a promising direction towards this objective. However, the relationship between these psychological constructs and their representations within LLMs remains underexplored and requires further investigation. Moreover, it is intriguing to understand and study the use of these representations to steer the models' behaviour. We propose a novel pipeline that extracts hidden state activations from transformer layers using the Big Five Personality Traits (Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness and Neuroticism), which is a comprehensive and empirically validated framework to model human personality applies low-rank subspace discovery methods, and identifies trait-specific optimal layers across different model architectures for robust injection. The resulting personality-aligned directions are then operationalised through a flexible steering framework with dynamic layer selection, enabling precise control of trait expression in LLM outputs. Our findings reveal that personality traits occupy a low-rank shared subspace, and that these latent structures can be transformed into actionable mechanisms for effective steering through careful perturbations without impacting the fluency, variance and general capabilities, helping to bridge the gap between psychological theory and practical model alignment.

papers.title: Localizing Persona Representations in LLMs
papers.research_question: Where in the model are persona representations encoded, and how do these representations vary across different personas?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that persona representations in LLMs are most strongly encoded in the final third of decoder layers, with political ideologies having distinct activations while ethical perspectives show polysemantic overlap.
papers.conclusion: The study localizes persona representations in LLMs, showing encoding in later layers and differences in distinctiveness between political and ethical personas, which can inform model interpretability and control.
papers.key_findings:
Final third of layers capture the most variance in persona representations across multiple LLMs.
Political views have distinctly localized activations, while ethical values exhibit higher activation overlap.
Llama3 shows the largest separation across layers and personas.
Deep Scan identified salient activations that are useful for detecting persona-specific sentences.
Overlap in activations suggests polysemanticity in ethical representations.
papers.limitation:
Analysis is specific to selected datasets and may not generalize to other data sources.
Datasets are in English and reflect WEIRD perspectives, limiting cultural diversity.
future_direction: Explore a wider range of models and personas.
Incorporate beliefs from more diverse cultural contexts.
Investigate controlled modifications of internal representations.
papers.abstract: We present a study on how and where personas -- defined by distinct sets of human characteristics, values, and beliefs -- are encoded in the representation space of large language models (LLMs). Using a range of dimension reduction and pattern recognition methods, we first identify the model layers that show the greatest divergence in encoding these representations. We then analyze the activations within a selected layer to examine how specific personas are encoded relative to others, including their shared and distinct embedding spaces. We find that, across multiple pre-trained decoder-only LLMs, the analyzed personas show large differences in representation space only within the final third of the decoder layers. We observe overlapping activations for specific ethical perspectives -- such as moral nihilism and utilitarianism -- suggesting a degree of polysemy. In contrast, political ideologies like conservatism and liberalism appear to be represented in more distinct regions. These findings help to improve our understanding of how LLMs internally represent information and can inform future efforts in refining the modulation of specific human traits in LLM outputs. Warning: This paper includes potentially offensive sample statements.

papers.title: From Black Boxes to Transparent Minds: Evaluating and Enhancing the Theory of Mind in Multimodal Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we evaluate and enhance Theory of Mind (ToM) capabilities in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) from an interpretability perspective?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces GridToM, a novel multimodal dataset for evaluating Theory of Mind (ToM), analyzes internal attention representations in MLLMs to show they distinguish perspective information, and proposes a training-free intervention method that enhances ToM performance by shifting activations along specific attention head directions.
papers.conclusion: The analysis of internal mechanisms shows that MLLMs develop attention heads capable of distinguishing perspective information and reasoning about beliefs, and targeted interventions based on these representations can significantly enhance their exhibited Theory of Mind capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads in multimodal large language models can distinguish cognitive information across different perspectives, providing evidence of internal Theory of Mind representations.
A training-free intervention method, which adjusts activations in the direction of sensitive attention heads, significantly improves model performance on first-order and second-order belief tasks.
Multimodal large language models perform better on text-based ToM tasks compared to video-only tasks.
Linear probing reveals that belief states are linearly separable in the activation space of attention heads, indicating structured internal representations.
The constructed GridToM dataset enables comprehensive and interpretability-driven evaluation of ToM capabilities in MLLMs.
papers.limitation:
The tasks in the dataset are limited to first-order and second-order belief tasks within the ATOMs framework, while ToM theory encompasses a broader range of unexplored tasks.
Due to restrictions in accessing model code, the approach was only validated on a limited selection of MLLMs.
papers.abstract: As large language models evolve, there is growing anticipation that they will emulate human-like Theory of Mind (ToM) to assist with routine tasks. However, existing methods for evaluating machine ToM focus primarily on unimodal models and largely treat these models as black boxes, lacking an interpretative exploration of their internal mechanisms. In response, this study adopts an approach based on internal mechanisms to provide an interpretability-driven assessment of ToM in multimodal large language models (MLLMs). Specifically, we first construct a multimodal ToM test dataset, GridToM, which incorporates diverse belief testing tasks and perceptual information from multiple perspectives. Next, our analysis shows that attention heads in multimodal large models can distinguish cognitive information across perspectives, providing evidence of ToM capabilities. Furthermore, we present a lightweight, training-free approach that significantly enhances the model's exhibited ToM by adjusting in the direction of the attention head.

papers.title: Probing then Editing Response Personality of Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How are personality traits encoded in the parameters of large language models, and can they be edited through layer-wise perturbations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a layer-wise probing framework to analyze personality encoding in LLMs and a perturbation method to edit personality during inference.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that personality traits are encoded in LLM layers and can be effectively edited through layer-wise perturbations.
papers.key_findings:
Personality knowledge emerges in middle layers and stabilizes in upper layers of LLMs.
Instruction-tuned models show clearer separation of personality traits.
The editing method can alter response personality even under contradictory prompts.
Difficulty of converting between personality traits aligns with representational distances.
The method incurs minimal degradation in general capabilities and has low overhead.
future_direction: Further investigation and leveraging of LLMs' capabilities to simulate personality.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated promising capabilities to generate responses that simulate consistent personality traits. Despite the major attempts to analyze personality expression through output-based evaluations, little is known about how such traits are internally encoded within LLM parameters. In this paper, we introduce a layer-wise probing framework to systematically investigate the layer-wise capability of LLMs in simulating personality for responding. We conduct probing experiments on 11 open-source LLMs over the PersonalityEdit benchmark and find that LLMs predominantly simulate personality for responding in their middle and upper layers, with instruction-tuned models demonstrating a slightly clearer separation of personality traits. Furthermore, by interpreting the trained probing hyperplane as a layer-wise boundary for each personality category, we propose a layer-wise perturbation method to edit the personality expressed by LLMs during inference. Our results show that even when the prompt explicitly specifies a particular personality, our method can still successfully alter the response personality of LLMs. Interestingly, the difficulty of converting between certain personality traits varies substantially, which aligns with the representational distances in our probing experiments. Finally, we conduct a comprehensive MMLU benchmark evaluation and time overhead analysis, demonstrating that our proposed personality editing method incurs only minimal degradation in general capabilities while maintaining low training costs and acceptable inference latency. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/universe-sky/probing-then-editing-personality.

papers.title: Linear Personality Probing and Steering in LLMs: A Big Five Study
papers.research_question: Whether linear directions aligned with the Big Five personality traits can be used for probing and steering model behavior in large language models.
papers.core_contribution: Linear directions aligned with Big Five traits are effective for personality probing, but steering is context-dependent, working well in forced-choice tasks but limited in open-ended generation or when prompt context is present.
papers.conclusion: Personality-related signals are embedded in the model's representational geometry, but steering vectors show strong context-dependency and are easily overridden by prompt context.
papers.key_findings:
Linear directions derived from regression align with Big Five traits and generalize to trait-relevant adjectives.
Steering with these vectors reliably shifts responses in forced-choice personality assessments.
Steering effects are overridden by explicit personality cues in the prompt.
Steering has minimal effect in open-ended generation tasks.
Regression-derived directions are more effective than SVD-derived directions for steering.
papers.limitation:
Steering effects are overridden by explicit personality cues in the prompt.
Steering is difficult to measure in open-ended generation where clear evaluation metrics are unavailable.
Aggregation across items and characters may obscure personality signals.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit distinct and consistent personalities that greatly impact trust and engagement. While this means that personality frameworks would be highly valuable tools to characterize and control LLMs' behavior, current approaches remain either costly (post-training) or brittle (prompt engineering). Probing and steering via linear directions has recently emerged as a cheap and efficient alternative. In this paper, we investigate whether linear directions aligned with the Big Five personality traits can be used for probing and steering model behavior. Using Llama 3.3 70B, we generate descriptions of 406 fictional characters and their Big Five trait scores. We then prompt the model with these descriptions and questions from the Alpaca questionnaire, allowing us to sample hidden activations that vary along personality traits in known, quantifiable ways. Using linear regression, we learn a set of per-layer directions in activation space, and test their effectiveness for probing and steering model behavior. Our results suggest that linear directions aligned with trait-scores are effective probes for personality detection, while their steering capabilities strongly depend on context, producing reliable effects in forced-choice tasks but limited influence in open-ended generation or when additional context is present in the prompt.

papers.title: When Truth Is Overridden: Uncovering the Internal Origins of Sycophancy in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How does sycophantic behavior arise within the internal mechanisms of Large Language Models?
papers.core_contribution: Sycophancy in LLMs arises from a two-stage process in late layers: a preference shift towards the user's opinion and a deeper representational divergence, while user expertise claims are not internally encoded and thus have minimal impact.
papers.conclusion: Sycophancy is not a surface-level artifact but emerges from a structural override of learned knowledge in deeper layers, with implications for alignment and truthful AI systems.
papers.key_findings:
User opinions strongly induce sycophancy, while expertise framing has minimal impact.
Sycophancy emerges in two stages: a late-layer output preference shift and a deeper representational divergence.
Activation patching confirms the causal role of late-layer representations in sycophantic behavior.
Expertise levels are not encoded internally, as their representations overlap, unlike opinion prompts which form distinct clusters.
First-person prompts induce higher sycophancy than third-person prompts due to stronger representational perturbations in deeper layers.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often exhibit sycophantic behavior, agreeing with user-stated opinions even when those contradict factual knowledge. While prior work has documented this tendency, the internal mechanisms that enable such behavior remain poorly understood. In this paper, we provide a mechanistic account of how sycophancy arises within LLMs. We first systematically study how user opinions induce sycophancy across different model families. We find that simple opinion statements reliably induce sycophancy, whereas user expertise framing has a negligible impact. Through logit-lens analysis and causal activation patching, we identify a two-stage emergence of sycophancy: (1) a late-layer output preference shift and (2) deeper representational divergence. We also verify that user authority fails to influence behavior because models do not encode it internally. In addition, we examine how grammatical perspective affects sycophantic behavior, finding that first-person prompts (``I believe...'') consistently induce higher sycophancy rates than third-person framings (``They believe...'') by creating stronger representational perturbations in deeper layers. These findings highlight that sycophancy is not a surface-level artifact but emerges from a structural override of learned knowledge in deeper layers, with implications for alignment and truthful AI systems.

papers.title: The Hydra Effect: Emergent Self-repair in Language Model Computations
papers.research_question: What is the internal computational structure of language models, and how do they respond to ablations? The paper investigates self-repair mechanisms (Hydra effect) and erasure functions in MLP layers.
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies two internal self-repair motifs in language models: the Hydra effect (downstream attention layers compensate for ablated layers) and erasure by late MLP layers (which downregulate the maximum-likelihood token).
papers.conclusion: The Hydra effect and erasure MLPs complicate circuit-level attribution and have implications for interpretability research, suggesting that assigning semantics to MLP neurons may be more difficult and that ablation studies must account for downstream compensatory changes.
papers.key_findings:
Language models exhibit the Hydra effect: ablating an attention layer causes a downstream attention layer to increase its impact to compensate.
Late MLP layers have an erasure function, acting to downregulate the maximum-likelihood token, and this effect is attenuated when attention layers are ablated.
Direct (unembedding-based) and total (ablation-based) importance measures are poorly correlated in most layers, except late layers.
The compensatory response is highly correlated with changes in direct effect at intermediate layers, explaining up to 92% of variance at layer 23.
These self-repair effects occur even in models trained without dropout, suggesting they are inherent to the architecture or training.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is performed at the layer level and does not investigate finer-grained components like individual attention heads or activation directions.
The compensatory effect does not fully restore the output, indicating that ablations still have a nonzero total effect.
future_direction: How much does the Hydra effect occur across the entire training distribution? Does sequence length play any role?
What are the Hydra effect attention heads responding to in the residual stream?
Do the same downstream heads act as Hydra effect replacement heads across multiple contexts?
papers.abstract: We investigate the internal structure of language model computations using causal analysis and demonstrate two motifs: (1) a form of adaptive computation where ablations of one attention layer of a language model cause another layer to compensate (which we term the Hydra effect) and (2) a counterbalancing function of late MLP layers that act to downregulate the maximum-likelihood token. Our ablation studies demonstrate that language model layers are typically relatively loosely coupled (ablations to one layer only affect a small number of downstream layers). Surprisingly, these effects occur even in language models trained without any form of dropout. We analyse these effects in the context of factual recall and consider their implications for circuit-level attribution in language models.

papers.title: GIM: Improved Interpretability for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How does self-repair, particularly within the attention mechanism, undermine the faithfulness of interpretability methods for large language models, and how can gradient-based attribution be modified to account for it?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies a novel form of self-repair within the attention mechanism (attention self-repair) and introduces GIM, a gradient-based attribution method that combines temperature-adjusted softmax gradients, layernorm freeze, and gradient normalization to account for self-repair and produce more faithful explanations.
papers.conclusion: GIM, by accounting for self-repair during backpropagation, advances the faithfulness of interpretability methods for transformers, providing a more accurate quantification of component importance and enhancing our understanding of neural network inner mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Attention self-repair is prevalent in LLMs, where softmax redistribution conceals the influence of important attention scores, leading gradient-based methods to underestimate component importance.
The proposed GIM method, which approximates the joint effect of perturbing multiple attention scores, significantly improves attribution faithfulness over existing gradient-based and circuit identification methods across multiple models and tasks.
All three modifications in GIM (TSG, layernorm freeze, grad norm) contribute to improved faithfulness, with layernorm freeze and gradient normalization having a particularly strong effect when combined.
GIM outperforms other methods in early transformer layers, which are critical for attention-based information routing.
TSG accurately approximates the effect of jointly ablating multiple attention scores during self-repair conditions, whereas standard gradients fail.
papers.limitation:
A causal link between TSG's mitigation of self-repair and the observed improvement in faithfulness cannot be conclusively established, as temperature adjustment affects backpropagation in multiple ways.
TSG decreased attribution faithfulness for the Qwen-2.5 1.5B model, potentially due to its hundred-fold larger gradients, but no definitive explanation was found.
future_direction: Investigate methods to estimate whether a perturbation will cause changes in multiple interacting attention scores, enabling a more principled selection between joint and individual effect estimation.
Empirically evaluate whether models trained with GIM-modified gradients demonstrate faster convergence or better performance.
papers.abstract: Ensuring faithful interpretability in large language models is imperative for trustworthy and reliable AI. A key obstacle is self-repair, a phenomenon where networks compensate for reduced signal in one component by amplifying others, masking the true importance of the ablated component. While prior work attributes self-repair to layer normalization and back-up components that compensate for ablated components, we identify a novel form occurring within the attention mechanism, where softmax redistribution conceals the influence of important attention scores. This leads traditional ablation and gradient-based methods to underestimate the significance of all components contributing to these attention scores. We introduce Gradient Interaction Modifications (GIM), a technique that accounts for self-repair during backpropagation. Extensive experiments across multiple large language models (Gemma 2B/9B, LLAMA 1B/3B/8B, Qwen 1.5B/3B) and diverse tasks demonstrate that GIM significantly improves faithfulness over existing circuit identification and feature attribution methods. Our work is a significant step toward better understanding the inner mechanisms of LLMs, which is crucial for improving them and ensuring their safety. Our code is available at https://github.com/JoakimEdin/gim.

papers.title: A Comprehensive Review of Large Language Models: Architecture, Types, Challenges, and Future Directions
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a comprehensive review of Large Language Models, covering their architecture, types, applications, challenges, and future directions.
papers.conclusion: While LLMs hold transformative potential, realizing their long-term societal benefits requires continued progress toward more reliable, efficient, and ethically aligned systems.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs are primarily based on the Transformer architecture, which uses self-attention mechanisms for contextual understanding and long-range dependencies.
LLMs have broad applications across domains such as content production, conversational systems, decision support, medicine, finance, and scientific research.
Key challenges faced by LLMs include hallucination, context limitations, computational demands, data quality issues, biases, and lack of interpretability.
Future research directions include multimodal integration, retrieval-augmented generation, agentic systems, and improvements in interpretability, alignment, and safety.
The evolution from encoder-decoder to decoder-only models has shaped modern generative LLMs, with decoder-only models like GPT becoming dominant for generative tasks.
future_direction: multimodal integration
retrieval-augmented generation techniques
development of agentic systems
interpretability, alignment, and safety research
papers.abstract: “LLM play a big role are they how generate AI is improving today.” Their success is highly attributed to the Transformer architecture, which uses self-attention mechanisms and large-scale training corpora to model complex linguistic dependencies and long-range relationships. This review synthesizes the theoretical foundations that underpin LLM design, emphasizing the role of self-attention in contextual understanding and outlining the structural distinctions between encoder–decoder systems and modern decoder-only generative models. The paper further investigates practical applications of LLMs across domains such as content production, conversational systems, decision support, and specialized analytical workflows. Despite their capabilities, LLMs face persistent challenges including hallucination, context limitations, computational demands, and issues of trustworthiness. People are concerned that the system might be unfair or biased, fairness, transparency, and interpretability continue to influence are they deployment take decisions. Looking ahead, the field is shaped by emerging trends including multimodal expansion, efficiency-oriented model compression, retrieval-augmented techniques for factual grounding, and the development of agentic systems capable of autonomous task execution. While LLMs hold transformative potential, realizing their long-term societal benefits requires continued progress toward more reliable, efficient, and ethically aligned systems.

papers.title: Inspection and Control of Self-Generated-Text Recognition Ability in Llama3-8b-Instruct
papers.research_question: Does self-generated text recognition robustly occur in LLMs, how is the behavior achieved, and can it be controlled?
papers.core_contribution: Isolated a vector in the residual stream causally related to self-recognition of text, and demonstrated it can be used to control the model's behavior and perception of authorship.
papers.conclusion: The chat model's self-recognition ability is likely learned during post-training, and the isolated vector explains its implementation and enables control over the behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Llama3-8b-Instruct reliably distinguishes its own outputs from human outputs, but the base model cannot.
The model does not rely on text perplexity for self-recognition.
A vector in the residual stream (layer 16) is differentially activated for self-written texts and is causally related to self-recognition.
Steering with this vector can control the model to claim or deny authorship of texts.
Coloring input texts with the vector can alter the model's perception of authorship.
papers.limitation:
There may be undetected identifying 'tells' in the texts used, though the Individual presentation paradigm is harder to explain away.
The vector may not capture all signals about writing characteristics.
future_direction: Using the vector to build resistance to jailbreaks and other safety risks.
Applying the findings to larger models and other model families.
papers.abstract: It has been reported that LLMs can recognize their own writing. As this has potential implications for AI safety, yet is relatively understudied, we investigate the phenomenon, seeking to establish whether it robustly occurs at the behavioral level, how the observed behavior is achieved, and whether it can be controlled. First, we find that the Llama3-8b-Instruct chat model - but not the base Llama3-8b model - can reliably distinguish its own outputs from those of humans, and present evidence that the chat model is likely using its experience with its own outputs, acquired during post-training, to succeed at the writing recognition task. Second, we identify a vector in the residual stream of the model that is differentially activated when the model makes a correct self-written-text recognition judgment, show that the vector activates in response to information relevant to self-authorship, present evidence that the vector is related to the concept of "self" in the model, and demonstrate that the vector is causally related to the model's ability to perceive and assert self-authorship. Finally, we show that the vector can be used to control both the model's behavior and its perception, steering the model to claim or disclaim authorship by applying the vector to the model's output as it generates it, and steering the model to believe or disbelieve it wrote arbitrary texts by applying the vector to them as the model reads them.

papers.title: Artificial Impressions: Evaluating Large Language Model Behavior Through the Lens of Trait Impressions
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether LLMs' internal representations encode impressions of prompt authors according to the Stereotype Content Model, and how these impressions predict downstream behavior and are influenced by prompt features.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces artificial impressions measured via linear probes on LLM hidden states, showing that these impressions are decodable, align with human perceptions, and predict model behavior such as response quality and hedging.
papers.conclusion: Artificial impressions provide a framework for studying LLM behavior and biases, revealing how prompt features influence model perceptions and outputs.
papers.key_findings:
LLM-reported impressions are biased toward positive traits and unreliable.
Linguistic patterns associated with warmth and competence in LLM-generated messages align with human perceptions.
Artificial impressions are linearly decodable from LLM hidden representations with high accuracy.
Models more clearly encode warmth than competence, mimicking human warmth primacy.
Warmth and competence impressions predict LLM response quality, and low competence predicts hedging in responses.
papers.abstract: We introduce and study artificial impressions--patterns in LLMs' internal representations of prompts that resemble human impressions and stereotypes based on language. We fit linear probes on generated prompts to predict impressions according to the two-dimensional Stereotype Content Model (SCM). Using these probes, we study the relationship between impressions and downstream model behavior as well as prompt features that may inform such impressions. We find that LLMs inconsistently report impressions when prompted, but also that impressions are more consistently linearly decodable from their hidden representations. Additionally, we show that artificial impressions of prompts are predictive of the quality and use of hedging in model responses. We also investigate how particular content, stylistic, and dialectal features in prompts impact LLM impressions.

papers.title: Open Sesame: Getting inside BERT’s Linguistic Knowledge
papers.research_question: How and to what extent does BERT encode syntactically-sensitive hierarchical information or positionally-sensitive linear information?
papers.core_contribution: BERT encodes positional information in lower layers and switches to a hierarchically-oriented encoding on higher layers. The paper also introduces a 'confusion score' to quantify intrusion effects in BERT's self-attention mechanism.
papers.conclusion: BERT composes increasingly abstract hierarchical representations of linguistic structure using self-attention, but does not show the sharp sensitivity to hierarchical structure found in human processing.
papers.key_findings:
Diagnostic classifiers show BERT's lower layers encode positional information well, while higher layers encode hierarchical information.
The proposed confusion score reveals BERT's attention is sensitive to syntactic structure and grammatical features (number, gender) in subject-verb agreement and reflexive anaphora.
BERT's attention is not perfectly syntactic; it sometimes attends to grammatically inaccessible or mismatched distractors.
Confusion scores decrease with layer depth, and there is an increase in confusion at layer 4, coinciding with the degradation of positional information.
BERT's performance on possessive constructions in the subject noun task is poor, possibly due to ambiguity of the 's token.
papers.limitation:
BERT performed poorly on possessive constructions in the subject noun task, possibly due to ambiguity of the 's token.
BERT's attention is only incompletely modulated by structural and featural properties, and attention is sometimes spread across grammatically irrelevant elements.
future_direction: Investigate or visualize layer-on-layer changes in BERT’s structural and positional information, particularly between layers 3 and 4.
Retrieve the increasingly hierarchical representations of BERT across layers via the self-attention mechanism.
papers.abstract: How and to what extent does BERT encode syntactically-sensitive hierarchical information or positionally-sensitive linear information? Recent work has shown that contextual representations like BERT perform well on tasks that require sensitivity to linguistic structure. We present here two studies which aim to provide a better understanding of the nature of BERT's representations. The first of these focuses on the identification of structurally-defined elements using diagnostic classifiers, while the second explores BERT's representation of subject-verb agreement and anaphor-antecedent dependencies through a quantitative assessment of self-attention vectors. In both cases, we find that BERT encodes positional information about word tokens well on its lower layers, but switches to a hierarchically-oriented encoding on higher layers. We conclude then that BERT's representations do indeed model linguistically relevant aspects of hierarchical structure, though they do not appear to show the sharp sensitivity to hierarchical structure that is found in human processing of reflexive anaphora.

papers.title: Explorations of Self-Repair in Language Models
papers.research_question: Does self-repair exist across model families and sizes when ablating individual attention heads on the full training distribution, and what are the mechanisms behind it?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that self-repair exists across model families and sizes on the full pretraining distribution, and identifies two contributing mechanisms: changes in the LayerNorm scaling factor and sparse sets of neurons implementing anti-erasure.
papers.conclusion: Self-repair is a real phenomenon that complicates interpretability efforts, and the findings provide evidence for the Iterative Inference hypothesis as a framework that predicts self-repair.
papers.key_findings:
Self-repair exists across model families and sizes when ablating individual attention heads on the full training distribution.
Self-repair is imperfect and noisy, with the degree of compensation varying significantly across prompts.
A nontrivial fraction (around 30%) of self-repair can be attributed to changes in the final LayerNorm scaling factor.
Sparse sets of neurons in MLP layers implement anti-erasure, contributing to self-repair, but the specific neurons vary across prompts.
Self-repair complicates interpretability efforts that rely on ablation-based metrics.
papers.limitation:
Self-repair is imperfect and noisy, making it difficult to quantify precisely.
Ablations take models off-distribution, leading to unpredictable and hard-to-interpret consequences.
future_direction: Control how far from distribution causal interventions take the model, e.g., by avoiding zero ablation or freezing LayerNorm.
Use path patching instead of patching full components to reduce off-distribution effects.
Further investigate the Iterative Inference hypothesis as an explanation for self-repair.
papers.abstract: Prior interpretability research studying narrow distributions has preliminarily identified self-repair, a phenomena where if components in large language models are ablated, later components will change their behavior to compensate. Our work builds off this past literature, demonstrating that self-repair exists on a variety of models families and sizes when ablating individual attention heads on the full training distribution. We further show that on the full training distribution self-repair is imperfect, as the original direct effect of the head is not fully restored, and noisy, since the degree of self-repair varies significantly across different prompts (sometimes overcorrecting beyond the original effect). We highlight two different mechanisms that contribute to self-repair, including changes in the final LayerNorm scaling factor and sparse sets of neurons implementing Anti-Erasure. We additionally discuss the implications of these results for interpretability practitioners and close with a more speculative discussion on the mystery of why self-repair occurs in these models at all, highlighting evidence for the Iterative Inference hypothesis in language models, a framework that predicts self-repair.

papers.title: Brittle Minds, Fixable Activations: Understanding Belief Representations in Language Models
papers.research_question: How do internal belief representations emerge in language models? Are they structured or spurious? How robust are they to prompt variations? Can they be strengthened?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides evidence that belief representations in language models improve with model size and fine-tuning, are structured yet brittle to prompt variations, and can be strengthened using contrastive activation addition to correct wrong Theory of Mind inferences.
papers.conclusion: Belief representations in language models are structured but brittle, and they can be strengthened via activation editing, offering a path toward more reliable Theory of Mind reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Belief representations emerge in consistent patterns across models, improve with model size, and benefit significantly from fine-tuning, especially in smaller models.
Control tasks and PCA show that belief representations are structured and not spurious.
Representations of others' beliefs are brittle to semantically neutral prompt variations.
Contrastive activation addition (CAA) can strengthen belief representations and improve ToM performance across different tasks.
CAA steering vectors are general and transferable to other ToM tasks, yielding substantial performance gains.
papers.limitation:
The study focused on one dataset (BigToM) and a limited set of model families due to computational constraints.
The approach could be extended to other mental states beyond beliefs.
future_direction: Exploring how different types of fine-tuning influence the emergence of internal belief representations.
Developing robustness benchmarks and new approaches to improve generalization of belief representations.
Directly embedding perspective-taking circuits into model architectures.
papers.abstract: Despite growing interest in Theory of Mind (ToM) tasks for evaluating language models (LMs), little is known about how LMs internally represent mental states of self and others. Understanding these internal mechanisms is critical - not only to move beyond surface-level performance, but also for model alignment and safety, where subtle misattributions of mental states may go undetected in generated outputs. In this work, we present the first systematic investigation of belief representations in LMs by probing models across different scales, training regimens, and prompts - using control tasks to rule out confounds. Our experiments provide evidence that both model size and fine-tuning substantially improve LMs' internal representations of others' beliefs, which are structured - not mere by-products of spurious correlations - yet brittle to prompt variations. Crucially, we show that these representations can be strengthened: targeted edits to model activations can correct wrong ToM inferences.

papers.title: The underlying structures of self-attention: symmetry, directionality, and emergent dynamics in Transformer training
papers.research_question: How can we interpret the structures learned in self-attention matrices, and what is the impact of different objective functions (autoregressive vs. bidirectional) on these matrices?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a mathematical framework linking self-attention matrices to bilinear forms, demonstrating that bidirectional training induces symmetry in weight matrices while autoregressive training results in directionality and column dominance. It applies these insights to show symmetric initialization improves encoder-only model performance.
papers.conclusion: The mathematical framework provides a novel theoretical perspective on how information is embedded through self-attention, improving the interpretability of Transformer models and offering practical benefits for model initialization.
papers.key_findings:
Autoregressive training induces directionality, producing columns with disproportionately high norms in the self-attention matrix Wqk.
Bidirectional training induces symmetric structures in the self-attention matrix Wqk.
These structural patterns (symmetry in encoder-only, directionality in decoder-only) are validated across diverse Transformer architectures and input modalities (text, vision, audio).
Symmetric initialization of Wqk improves training efficiency and final performance for encoder-only language models, leading to faster convergence and lower loss.
Symmetric initialization did not yield similar benefits for vision transformer models under the tested conditions.
papers.limitation: Symmetric initialization did not result in faster convergence or improved final performance for vision transformer models, in contrast to the gains observed in language models.
papers.abstract: Self-attention is essential to Transformer architectures, yet how information is embedded in the self-attention matrices and how different objective functions impact this process remains unclear. We present a mathematical framework to analyze self-attention matrices by deriving the structures governing their weight updates. Using this framework, we demonstrate that bidirectional training induces symmetry in the weight matrices, while autoregressive training results in directionality and column dominance. Our theoretical findings are validated across multiple Transformer models - including ModernBERT, GPT, LLaMA3, and Mistral - and input modalities like text, vision, and audio. Finally, we apply these insights by showing that symmetric initialization improves the performance of encoder-only models on language tasks. This mathematical analysis offers a novel theoretical perspective on how information is embedded through self-attention, thereby improving the interpretability of Transformer models.

papers.title: Anchors in the Machine: Behavioral and Attributional Evidence of Anchoring Bias in LLMs
papers.research_question: Does anchoring bias in LLMs reflect surface imitation or deeper probability shifts in internal mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Integrates log-probability-based behavioral analysis with exact Shapley-value attribution to measure anchoring bias in LLMs, introducing an Anchoring Bias Sensitivity Score.
papers.conclusion: Anchoring bias in LLMs is robust and quantifiable, with implications for using LLMs as decision systems and for interpretability research.
papers.key_findings:
Robust anchoring effects are observed in Gemma-2B, Phi-2, and Llama-2-7B, with attribution showing that anchors influence reweighting.
Smaller models like GPT-2, Falcon-RW-1B, and GPT-Neo-125M show variability in anchoring sensitivity, suggesting scale may modulate effects.
Attributional effects vary across prompt designs, indicating fragility in treating LLMs as human substitutes.
The Anchoring Bias Sensitivity Score (ABSS) ranks models based on combined behavioral and attributional evidence.
Behavioral anchoring is consistent across models, but attribution alignment can be discordant, especially in smaller models.
papers.limitation:
Discretization of outputs to fixed numeric strings
No mechanistic claims as internal parameters and circuits were not probed
Method only works for models with open log-probabilities of outputs
future_direction: Expanding to a broader set of models
Integrating attributional evidence with concept-based and mechanistic interpretability
Extending the methodology to other cognitive biases
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly examined as both behavioral subjects and decision systems, yet it remains unclear whether observed cognitive biases reflect surface imitation or deeper probability shifts. Anchoring bias, a classic human judgment bias, offers a critical test case. While prior work shows LLMs exhibit anchoring, most evidence relies on surface-level outputs, leaving internal mechanisms and attributional contributions unexplored. This paper advances the study of anchoring in LLMs through three contributions: (1) a log-probability-based behavioral analysis showing that anchors shift entire output distributions, with controls for training-data contamination; (2) exact Shapley-value attribution over structured prompt fields to quantify anchor influence on model log-probabilities; and (3) a unified Anchoring Bias Sensitivity Score integrating behavioral and attributional evidence across six open-source models. Results reveal robust anchoring effects in Gemma-2B, Phi-2, and Llama-2-7B, with attribution signaling that the anchors influence reweighting. Smaller models such as GPT-2, Falcon-RW-1B, and GPT-Neo-125M show variability, suggesting scale may modulate sensitivity. Attributional effects, however, vary across prompt designs, underscoring fragility in treating LLMs as human substitutes. The findings demonstrate that anchoring bias in LLMs is robust, measurable, and interpretable, while highlighting risks in applied domains. More broadly, the framework bridges behavioral science, LLM safety, and interpretability, offering a reproducible path for evaluating other cognitive biases in LLMs.

papers.title: Sycophancy Is Not One Thing: Causal Separation of Sycophantic Behaviors in LLMs
papers.research_question: Whether sycophantic behaviors (excessive agreement and flattery) in LLMs arise from a single mechanism or multiple distinct processes, specifically if sycophantic agreement, genuine agreement, and sycophantic praise are distinct and independently steerable.
papers.core_contribution: Sycophantic behaviors (agreement and praise) are encoded along distinct linear directions in model representations and can be independently steered, indicating that sycophancy is not a single construct but a family of separable behaviors.
papers.conclusion: Sycophancy should be reframed as a family of distinct behaviors with separable internal representations; evaluations and interventions must be behavior-specific rather than treating sycophancy as a single phenomenon.
papers.key_findings:
Sycophantic agreement, genuine agreement, and sycophantic praise each correspond to distinct subspaces in model representations.
These behaviors are independently steerable via activation addition along learned difference-in-means directions, demonstrating functional separability.
The same representational structure for these behaviors appears consistently across different model families and scales.
Early layers encode a generic agreement signal that conflates sycophantic and genuine agreement, which diverge into distinct directions in later layers.
Sycophantic praise is encoded orthogonally to agreement behaviors across all layers.
papers.limitation:
The study only examines three sycophancy-related behaviors (sycophantic agreement, genuine agreement, sycophantic praise), not the full spectrum of sycophantic behaviors such as emotional validation or mimicry.
External validation for praise is limited because existing naturalistic benchmarks (e.g., SycophancyEval, SYCON-Bench) primarily test agreement-based deference and lack a direct ecological benchmark for praise.
Evidence is restricted to linear analyses of the residual stream (difference-in-means, activation addition, subspace removal) and does not test nonlinear methods or interventions at other network sites.
future_direction: Test whether the same separable structure appears under nonlinear analysis methods, in attention or MLP activations, and in other model families or training regimes.
Extend the analysis to a broader range of sycophancy-related behaviors such as emotional validation, acceptance framing, and mimicry.
Develop naturalistic benchmarks that directly target praise or flattery to better validate the external validity of praise-related findings.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often exhibit sycophantic behaviors -- such as excessive agreement with or flattery of the user -- but it is unclear whether these behaviors arise from a single mechanism or multiple distinct processes. We decompose sycophancy into sycophantic agreement and sycophantic praise, contrasting both with genuine agreement. Using difference-in-means directions, activation additions, and subspace geometry across multiple models and datasets, we show that: (1) the three behaviors are encoded along distinct linear directions in latent space; (2) each behavior can be independently amplified or suppressed without affecting the others; and (3) their representational structure is consistent across model families and scales. These results suggest that sycophantic behaviors correspond to distinct, independently steerable representations.

papers.title: Breaking the Mirror: Activation-Based Mitigation of Self-Preference in LLM Evaluators
papers.research_question: Can lightweight steering vectors mitigate self-preference bias in LLM evaluators at inference time without retraining?
papers.core_contribution: Steering vectors can reduce unjustified self-preference bias by up to 97%, outperforming prompting and DPO baselines, but are unstable on legitimate self-preference and unbiased agreement.
papers.conclusion: Steering vectors show promise for mitigating self-preference bias but have limitations, motivating more robust interventions.
papers.key_findings:
Steering vectors reduce illegitimate self-preference bias by up to 97%.
They substantially outperform prompting and DPO baselines.
Steering vectors are unstable on legitimate self-preference and unbiased agreement.
Self-preference may have a linear representation in activation space.
Optimization-based steering performs comparably to CAA with fewer examples.
papers.limitation:
Vectors are not robust to legitimate self-preference and unbiased agreement cases.
Ordering bias in pairwise setting confounds CAA method.
future_direction: Explore whether illegitimate self-preference is linearly encoded while other cases are different directions.
Incorporate individual rather than pairwise evaluations to circumvent ordering bias.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly serve as automated evaluators, yet they suffer from "self-preference bias": a tendency to favor their own outputs over those of other models. This bias undermines fairness and reliability in evaluation pipelines, particularly for tasks like preference tuning and model routing. We investigate whether lightweight steering vectors can mitigate this problem at inference time without retraining. We introduce a curated dataset that distinguishes self-preference bias into justified examples of self-preference and unjustified examples of self-preference, and we construct steering vectors using two methods: Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) and an optimization-based approach. Our results show that steering vectors can reduce unjustified self-preference bias by up to 97\%, substantially outperforming prompting and direct preference optimization baselines. Yet steering vectors are unstable on legitimate self-preference and unbiased agreement, implying self-preference spans multiple or nonlinear directions. This underscores both their promise and limits as safeguards for LLM-as-judges and motivates more robust interventions.

papers.title: Can Role Vectors Affect LLM Behaviour?
papers.research_question: Can we identify role vectors in the activation space that improve performance on objective tasks? Do these directions effectively impersonate the role of interest? Does ablating these directions degrade performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces role vectors, a method to steer LLM behavior by manipulating internal activations, showing that this approach improves in-domain and cross-domain task performance more effectively than persona-based prompting.
papers.conclusion: Role vectors can effectively steer LLM behavior and improve performance on objective tasks, providing a more direct and effective control mechanism than persona-based prompting.
papers.key_findings:
Role vectors can be identified and used to improve performance on domain-specific tasks, with in-domain improvements and unexpected cross-domain gains.
Ablating the role vectors degrades performance, indicating their causal role in the model's behavior.
The effect of role vectors is more consistent and substantial than traditional persona-based prompting.
The results support the linear representation hypothesis, showing that high-level concepts are linearly represented in the activation space.
The method generalizes across multiple models and domains, as shown by cross-dataset validation on MedQA.
papers.abstract: The influence of personas on Large Language Models (LLMs) has been widely studied, yet their direct impact on performance remains uncertain. This work explores a novel approach to guiding LLM behaviour through role vectors, an alternative to persona-based prompting. We construct 29 role vectors derived from model activations and evaluate their impact on benchmark performance across multiple domains. Our analysis investigates whether these vectors can effectively steer models toward domain-specific expertise. We measure two key interventions: (i) activation addition, which reinforces role-specific directions, and (ii) directional ablation, which removes them. Results on well-established benchmarks indicate that role vectors do, in fact, influence model behaviour, improving in-domain task performance while also yielding unexpected cross-domain gains. This, in turn, suggests that manipulating internal model representations has a greater impact on outcomes than persona-based prompting.

papers.title: Human-like Social Compliance in Large Language Models: Unifying Sycophancy and Conformity through Signal Competition Dynamics
papers.research_question: What is the shared mechanism behind sycophancy and conformity in LLMs, and how does the interplay of signal competition and confidence govern compliance?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Signal Competition Mechanism, a unified framework showing that sycophancy and conformity in LLMs arise from a shared compliance subspace where social signals override internal knowledge through deterministic competition.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that LLM compliance is predictable via signal competition, revealing a systemic misalignment where social standards override epistemic standards, and proposes an Integrated Epistemic Alignment Framework for developing robust, truth-seeking agents.
papers.key_findings:
Sycophancy and conformity are behaviorally correlated across models, indicating a shared latent susceptibility.
Both behaviors originate from a convergent geometric manifold (compliance subspace) in the model's latent space, with high directional similarity in internal representations.
Compliance is a deterministic process governed by a linear boundary where the Social Emotional Signal overcomes the Information Calibration Signal (S > I).
The Confidence Margin provides an inertial barrier against social pressure, but it is permeable and insufficient to guarantee immunity under intense signals.
Models exhibit distinct resistance profiles: InternLM3 shows a sharp phase transition, Qwen2.5 has high baseline susceptibility, and Llama-3.1 has a noisy, gradual transition.
papers.limitation:
static nature of the evaluation datasets and focus on standard transformer paradigms
generalizability to implicit or multi-modal social manipulations and ultra-long context reasoning
future_direction: Extending findings to implicit social manipulations and ultra-long context reasoning
Implementing the Integrated Epistemic Alignment Framework for epistemic self-regulation
papers.abstract: The increasing integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into decision-making frameworks has exposed significant vulnerabilities to social compliance, specifically sycophancy and conformity. However, a critical research gap exists regarding the fundamental mechanisms that enable external social cues to systematically override a model's internal parametric knowledge. This study introduces the Signal Competition Mechanism, a unified framework validated by assessing behavioral correlations across 15 LLMs and performing latent-space probing on three representative open-source models. The analysis demonstrates that sycophancy and conformity originate from a convergent geometric manifold, hereafter termed the compliance subspace, which is characterized by high directional similarity in internal representations. Furthermore, the transition to compliance is shown to be a deterministic process governed by a linear boundary, where the Social Emotional Signal effectively suppresses the Information Calibration Signal. Crucially, we identify a "Transparency-Truth Gap," revealing that while internal confidence provides an inertial barrier, it remains permeable and insufficient to guarantee immunity against intense social pressure. By formalizing the Integrated Epistemic Alignment Framework, this research provides a blueprint for transitioning from instructional adherence to robust epistemic integrity.

papers.title: What Does BERT Learn about the Structure of Language?
papers.research_question: What linguistic structure does BERT learn? Specifically, can we unveil the representations learned by BERT to proto-linguistics structures?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides evidence that BERT captures hierarchical linguistic structure, with surface features in lower layers, syntactic in middle, and semantic in higher layers, and that it uses deeper layers for long-distance dependencies and implicitly captures tree-like structures.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that BERT captures structural properties of English language, with a hierarchy of linguistic signals and compositional modeling that parallels traditional syntactic analysis.
papers.key_findings:
BERT's phrasal representation captures phrase-level information in the lower layers, which gets diluted in higher layers.
BERT embeds a rich hierarchy of linguistic signals: surface information at the bottom, syntactic in the middle, and semantic at the top.
BERT requires deeper layers to handle long-distance dependency information, such as subject-verb agreement with more attractors.
BERT implicitly implements a tree-based compositional scheme, as shown by Tensor Product Decomposition Networks (TPDN) approximating BERT's representations.
The untrained version of BERT in higher layers outperforms the trained version in predicting sentence length, indicating that training trades off basic surface features for more complex information.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to English and may not generalize to other languages or noisy user-generated content.
future_direction: Investigating if the results transfer to other domains with higher syntactic variability, such as noisy user-generated content or morphologically-rich languages.
papers.abstract: BERT is a recent language representation model that has surprisingly performed well in diverse language understanding benchmarks. This result indicates the possibility that BERT networks capture structural information about language. In this work, we provide novel support for this claim by performing a series of experiments to unpack the elements of English language structure learned by BERT. We first show that BERT's phrasal representation captures phrase-level information in the lower layers. We also show that BERT's intermediate layers encode a rich hierarchy of linguistic information, with surface features at the bottom, syntactic features in the middle and semantic features at the top. BERT turns out to require deeper layers when long-distance dependency information is required, e.g. to track subjectverb agreement. Finally, we show that BERT representations capture linguistic information in a compositional way that mimics classical, tree-like structures.

papers.title: Interpretability in the Wild: a Circuit for Indirect Object Identification in GPT-2 small
papers.research_question: How does GPT-2 small perform the indirect object identification (IOI) task, and what internal circuit is responsible for this behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies and validates a circuit of 26 attention heads in GPT-2 small that performs indirect object identification, using a combination of interpretability techniques and quantitative criteria for faithfulness, completeness, and minimality.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that mechanistic understanding of large ML models is feasible, providing a step towards scaling interpretability to larger models and more complex tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Discovered a circuit of 26 attention heads grouped into 7 classes (e.g., Name Mover Heads, S-Inhibition Heads) that implement the IOI task.
Identified redundant behavior such as Backup Name Mover Heads that activate when regular Name Mover Heads are ablated.
