Pre-trained models can be re-parametrized into collaborative attention via tensor decomposition, allowing compression without retraining.
Collaborative attention consistently improves over concatenation-based attention with the same number of parameters.
The method is effective across modalities (text and image) and various transformer architectures (BERT, DistilBERT, ALBERT, DeiT).
papers.limitation: ALBERT suffers more from compression, possibly because it already shares parameters across layers, which may limit the redundancy that can be exploited.
papers.abstract: Attention layers are widely used in natural language processing (NLP) and are beginning to influence computer vision architectures. Training very large transformer models allowed significant improvement in both fields, but once trained, these networks show symptoms of over-parameterization. For instance, it is known that many attention heads can be pruned without impacting accuracy. This work aims to enhance current understanding on how multiple heads interact. Motivated by the observation that attention heads learn redundant key/query projections, we propose a collaborative multi-head attention layer that enables heads to learn shared projections. Our scheme decreases the number of parameters in an attention layer and can be used as a drop-in replacement in any transformer architecture. Our experiments confirm that sharing key/query dimensions can be exploited in language understanding, machine translation and vision. We also show that it is possible to re-parametrize a pre-trained multi-head attention layer into our collaborative attention layer. Collaborative multi-head attention reduces the size of the key and query projections by 4 for same accuracy and speed. Our code is public.

papers.title: Vision Transformers Need Registers
papers.research_question: Why do artifacts (high-norm tokens) appear in feature maps of vision transformers, and how can they be fixed?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies artifacts (high-norm tokens) in vision transformer feature maps and proposes a simple fix by adding register tokens to the input sequence, which removes artifacts and improves performance on dense prediction tasks and object discovery.
papers.conclusion: The paper exposes artifacts in vision transformer feature maps, proposes adding register tokens as a simple fix, and demonstrates its effectiveness across supervised, text-supervised, and self-supervised models.
papers.key_findings:
Artifacts correspond to high-norm tokens that appear primarily in low-informative background areas of images.
These high-norm tokens hold global image information but little local patch information.
Adding register tokens to the input sequence entirely removes the artifacts, leading to smoother feature and attention maps.
Models trained with register tokens show improved performance on dense prediction tasks like segmentation and depth estimation.
Register tokens enable object discovery methods (e.g., LOST) to work effectively with modern vision transformers.
papers.limitation: The authors have not been able to fully determine which aspects of the training led to the appearance of artifacts in different models.
future_direction: Study the regularization of registers.
Investigate why the value projection in OpenCLIP filters out outliers even without registers.
papers.abstract: Transformers have recently emerged as a powerful tool for learning visual representations. In this paper, we identify and characterize artifacts in feature maps of both supervised and self-supervised ViT networks. The artifacts correspond to high-norm tokens appearing during inference primarily in low-informative background areas of images, that are repurposed for internal computations. We propose a simple yet effective solution based on providing additional tokens to the input sequence of the Vision Transformer to fill that role. We show that this solution fixes that problem entirely for both supervised and self-supervised models, sets a new state of the art for self-supervised visual models on dense visual prediction tasks, enables object discovery methods with larger models, and most importantly leads to smoother feature maps and attention maps for downstream visual processing.

papers.title: Balancing Stylization and Truth via Disentangled Representation Steering
papers.research_question: What causes stylization-induced truthfulness collapse in representation editing for LLMs, and how can it be mitigated to preserve both style and truth?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces StyliTruth, a training-free representation editing method that disentangles style and truth subspaces in LLM activations to mitigate stylization-induced truthfulness collapse, enabling independent control of style and truth.
papers.conclusion: StyliTruth addresses stylization-induced truthfulness collapse by disentangling style and truth subspaces, preserving truthfulness while enabling effective stylistic control in LLM responses.
papers.key_findings:
Stylization-induced truthfulness collapse occurs due to entanglement of style and truth directions in certain attention heads.
StyliTruth effectively disentangles style and truth subspaces using orthogonal deflation and adaptive token-level editing.
Experiments show StyliTruth outperforms existing methods in balancing style adherence and truthfulness on multiple datasets.
Ablation studies confirm that both subspace disentanglement and adaptive token-level editing are crucial for performance.
Analysis demonstrates that StyliTruth successfully isolates style and truth subspaces, reducing interference.
papers.abstract: Generating stylized large language model (LLM) responses via representation editing is a promising way for fine-grained output control. However, there exists an inherent trade-off: imposing a distinctive style often degrades truthfulness. Existing representation editing methods, by naively injecting style signals, overlook this collateral impact and frequently contaminate the model's core truthfulness representations, resulting in reduced answer correctness. We term this phenomenon stylization-induced truthfulness collapse. We attribute this issue to latent coupling between style and truth directions in certain key attention heads, and propose StyliTruth, a mechanism that preserves stylization while keeping truthfulness intact. StyliTruth separates the style-relevant and truth-relevant subspaces in the model's representation space via an orthogonal deflation process. This decomposition enables independent control of style and truth in their own subspaces, minimizing interference. By designing adaptive, token-level steering vectors within each subspace, we dynamically and precisely control the generation process to maintain both stylistic fidelity and truthfulness. We validate our method on multiple styles and languages. Extensive experiments and analyses show that StyliTruth significantly reduces stylization-induced truthfulness collapse and outperforms existing inference-time intervention methods in balancing style adherence with truthfulness.

papers.title: Neural Transparency: Mechanistic Interpretability Interfaces for Anticipating Model Behaviors for Personalized AI
papers.research_question: Can neural transparency tools, which translate mechanistic interpretability insights into user-facing interfaces, help users anticipate and design safer AI chatbot behaviors from system prompts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a neural transparency interface that translates mechanistic interpretability insights (persona vectors derived from neural activations) into an actionable tool for non-technical users to predict chatbot personality traits from system prompts before deployment.
papers.conclusion: Neural transparency visualizations can increase user trust and enhance the subjective experience of the AI design process, offering a path to operationalize mechanistic interpretability for end-users to support safer, more aligned human-AI interactions.
papers.key_findings:
Users systematically miscalibrated their predictions of AI behavior, misjudging trait activations for 11 of 15 analyzable traits, highlighting the need for transparency tools.
The neural transparency interface significantly increased user trust in the AI model and was enthusiastically received, though it did not change design iteration patterns.
Persona vectors (linear directions in activation space) for traits like empathy, sociality, and toxicity showed strong linear relationships with synthetic prompt levels, validating the approach for most traits.
papers.limitation:
Relied on GPT-4.1-mini to evaluate trait expression in Llama responses, which may not fully capture human judgments of trait expression.
The persona vector generation method uses simple difference-in-means, prioritizing efficiency over the potential accuracy/robustness of more complex techniques like linear probes.
The 10-minute interaction period may not capture longer-term dynamics of chatbot relationships where problematic interactions typically emerge.
Participants' inaccurate trait predictions may be partly due to transforming coarse ordinal prediction data to normalized values, potentially making predictions more extreme.
future_direction: Longitudinal deployment studies to track users across multiple chatbot creation sessions.
Adversarial task conditions where transparency tools become necessary to avoid dangerous traits.
Active steering interfaces allowing users to directly manipulate persona vector activations.
Development of a standardized trait disclosure framework (like a 'nutritional label') for chatbots.
Studies with vulnerable populations (e.g., adolescents) most at risk from problematic chatbot relationships.
papers.abstract: Millions of users now design personalized LLM-based chatbots that shape their daily interactions, yet they can only roughly anticipate how their design choices will manifest as behaviors in deployment. This opacity is consequential: seemingly innocuous prompts can trigger excessive sycophancy, toxicity, or other undesirable traits, degrading utility and raising safety concerns. To address this issue, we introduce an interface that enables neural transparency by exposing language model internals during chatbot design. Our approach extracts behavioral trait vectors (empathy, toxicity, sycophancy, etc.) by computing differences in neural activations between contrastive system prompts that elicit opposing behaviors. We predict chatbot behaviors by projecting the system prompt's final token activations onto these trait vectors, normalizing for cross-trait comparability, and visualizing results via an interactive sunburst diagram. To evaluate this approach, we conducted an online user study using Prolific to compare our neural transparency interface against a baseline chatbot interface without any form of transparency. Our analyses suggest that users systematically miscalibrated AI behavior: participants misjudged trait activations for eleven of fifteen analyzable traits, motivating the need for transparency tools in everyday human-AI interaction. While our interface did not change design iteration patterns, it significantly increased user trust and was enthusiastically received. Qualitative analysis revealed nuanced user experiences with the visualization, suggesting interface and interaction improvements for future work. This work offers a path for how mechanistic interpretability can be operationalized for non-technical users, establishing a foundation for safer, more aligned human-AI interactions.

papers.title: HACK: Hallucinations Along Certainty and Knowledge Axes
papers.research_question: How can hallucinations in large language models be categorized based on the model's internal properties (knowledge and certainty) rather than external properties, and how can this categorization inform targeted mitigation strategies?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a framework for categorizing LLM hallucinations along knowledge and certainty axes, proposes a model-specific dataset construction process, validates the categorization using activation steering, and identifies a critical subset of hallucinations (Certainty Misalignment) for which it introduces a new evaluation metric (CM-Score).
papers.conclusion: The findings highlight the importance of considering both knowledge and certainty in hallucination analysis and call for targeted mitigation approaches that consider the hallucination's underlying factors.
papers.key_findings:
Hallucinations can be systematically categorized based on whether the model possesses the correct parametric knowledge (HK+ vs HK-) and its certainty (HC+ vs HC-).
Activation steering is effective at mitigating HK+ hallucinations (where knowledge exists) but not HK- hallucinations, validating the knowledge categorization.
A significant subset of hallucinations (9%–43%) are Certainty Misalignment (CM) cases, where the model hallucinates with high certainty despite having the correct knowledge internally.
Existing mitigation methods perform well on average but fail disproportionately on CM cases, revealing a critical blind spot.
Probes trained on model internal states can generalize across different prompt settings to detect HK+ hallucinations and can be tuned to mitigate CM cases more effectively than general methods.
papers.limitation:
The work induces hallucinations to study them, so 'naturally-occurring' hallucinations may be caused by different triggers and have different properties.
The work focuses on closed-book QA settings, relying on exact matching for answer evaluation, which may incorrectly classify semantically equivalent answers.
Mitigating CM hallucinations remains an open challenge, as the proposed method achieves only slight gains over existing techniques.
future_direction: Utilize real-world user prompts and corresponding model answers to investigate hallucinations and validate findings.
Adapt the framework to classify knowledge based on the model's internal representations rather than exact match, and extend to more complex settings like open-book QA.
Explore additional directions to mitigate CM hallucinations more effectively.
papers.abstract: Hallucinations in LLMs present a critical barrier to their reliable usage. Existing research usually categorizes hallucination by their external properties rather than by the LLMs' underlying internal properties. This external focus overlooks that hallucinations may require tailored mitigation strategies based on their underlying mechanism. We propose a framework for categorizing hallucinations along two axes: knowledge and certainty. Since parametric knowledge and certainty may vary across models, our categorization method involves a model-specific dataset construction process that differentiates between those types of hallucinations. Along the knowledge axis, we distinguish between hallucinations caused by a lack of knowledge and those occurring despite the model having the knowledge of the correct response. To validate our framework along the knowledge axis, we apply steering mitigation, which relies on the existence of parametric knowledge to manipulate model activations. This addresses the lack of existing methods to validate knowledge categorization by showing a significant difference between the two hallucination types. We further analyze the distinct knowledge and hallucination patterns between models, showing that different hallucinations do occur despite shared parametric knowledge. Turning to the certainty axis, we identify a particularly concerning subset of hallucinations where models hallucinate with certainty despite having the correct knowledge internally. We introduce a new evaluation metric to measure the effectiveness of mitigation methods on this subset, revealing that while some methods perform well on average, they fail disproportionately on these critical cases. Our findings highlight the importance of considering both knowledge and certainty in hallucination analysis and call for targeted mitigation approaches that consider the hallucination underlying factors.

papers.title: Localizing Lying in Llama: Understanding Instructed Dishonesty on True-False Questions Through Prompting, Probing, and Patching
papers.research_question: How can instructed dishonesty (lying) in a large language model be localized and understood using mechanistic interpretability methods?
papers.core_contribution: The paper localizes layers and attention heads responsible for instructed dishonesty in LLaMA-2-70b-chat, showing that causal interventions on just 46 heads can flip the model's behavior from lying to answering honestly.
papers.conclusion: The work contributes to understanding dishonesty in LLMs by localizing the behavior to specific layers and heads, enabling causal interventions that flip the model from lying to honesty, with the goal of informing methods to prevent such behavior.
papers.key_findings:
LLaMA-2-70b-chat can be instructed to lie on true/false questions, but this behavior is sensitive and requires careful prompt engineering, including the use of assistant response prefixes.
Linear probing and activation patching identify layers 19-23 as crucial for dishonest behavior, with representations between honest and liar prompts becoming anti-parallel after these layers.
Activation patching from an honest model into a lying model on layers 19-23 can significantly increase the liar's accuracy from 2% to 63%.
A subset of 46 attention heads within layers 19-23 (0.9% of all heads) is causally important for lying; patching these heads from honest to liar models flips the liar's behavior to be honest, and vice versa.
The intervention on the 46 heads generalizes robustly across different prompts and dataset splits (Cities, Inventions, Chemical Elements, Animals, Companies, Scientific Facts).
papers.limitation: The analysis is in a toy scenario where lying involves outputting a one-token incorrect response; realistic lying scenarios could involve arbitrarily misaligned optimization targets.
future_direction: Analyze more complex misalignments (e.g., swaying political beliefs, selling products) using similar methods to find where biases/misalignments exist.
Further mechanistic interpretability work to understand how the model elicits a truth-value representation and uses it with the system prompt to decide whether to respond truthfully.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate significant knowledge through their outputs, though it is often unclear whether false outputs are due to a lack of knowledge or dishonesty. In this paper, we investigate instructed dishonesty, wherein we explicitly prompt LLaMA-2-70b-chat to lie. We perform prompt engineering to find which prompts best induce lying behavior, and then use mechanistic interpretability approaches to localize where in the network this behavior occurs. Using linear probing and activation patching, we localize five layers that appear especially important for lying. We then find just 46 attention heads within these layers that enable us to causally intervene such that the lying model instead answers honestly. We show that these interventions work robustly across many prompts and dataset splits. Overall, our work contributes a greater understanding of dishonesty in LLMs so that we may hope to prevent it.

papers.title: Analysing Moral Bias in Finetuned LLMs through Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether LLMs exhibit the Knobe effect (a moral bias in intentionality judgments), whether specific Transformer layers encode this bias, and whether targeted interventions (layer-patching) can mitigate it.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that the Knobe effect (a moral bias) emerges in finetuned LLMs, is localized in mid-to-late Transformer layers, and can be mitigated by patching activations from pretrained models into finetuned models, without retraining.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that social biases in LLMs can be mechanistically localized and mitigated through targeted interventions like layer-patching, offering a method for model repair without retraining.
papers.key_findings:
Finetuned LLMs exhibit the Knobe effect (moral bias in intentionality judgments), while pretrained models show minimal effect.
The bias is localized in mid-to-late Transformer layers, as shown by differences in residual stream activations.
Patching activations from pretrained models into specific layers of finetuned models can reduce or eliminate the bias.
The mitigation via layer-patching does not significantly harm general model performance on standard benchmarks.
The Knobe effect is not an emergent property of model scale alone; it is induced by finetuning and appears across model sizes.
papers.limitation: The layer-patching method requires access to the pretrained model.
future_direction: Explore whether this localization technique applies to other biases, such as gender or racial stereotypes.
Develop methods that do not rely on access to the pretrained model.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been shown to internalize human-like biases during finetuning, yet the mechanisms by which these biases manifest remain unclear. In this work, we investigated whether the well-known Knobe effect, a moral bias in intentionality judgements, emerges in finetuned LLMs and whether it can be traced back to specific components of the model. We conducted a Layer-Patching analysis across 3 open-weights LLMs and demonstrated that the bias is not only learned during finetuning but also localized in a specific set of layers. Surprisingly, we found that patching activations from the corresponding pretrained model into just a few critical layers is sufficient to eliminate the effect. Our findings offer new evidence that social biases in LLMs can be interpreted, localized, and mitigated through targeted interventions, without the need for model retraining.

papers.title: Uncovering mesa-optimization algorithms in Transformers
papers.research_question: How does in-context learning emerge in autoregressive Transformers trained on next-token prediction? The paper investigates whether such training gives rise to a gradient-based optimization algorithm (mesa-optimizer) that adjusts the model as new inputs are revealed.
papers.core_contribution: Autoregressive Transformers trained on next-token prediction learn a gradient-based mesa-optimization algorithm that performs in-context learning, explaining the emergence of in-context learning and inspiring new Transformer layers.
papers.conclusion: In-context learning in autoregressive Transformers arises from mesa-optimization algorithms learned during training, which can be leveraged to design more efficient optimization-based layers.
papers.key_findings:
Early Transformer layers learn a token binding mechanism that aggregates consecutive observations into internal representations, enabling subsequent mesa-optimization.
Trained single-layer linear self-attention models implement one-step gradient descent on a least-squares objective, matching the theoretical construction.
Multi-layer linear self-attention models implement a preconditioned gradient descent algorithm that approximates the optimal least-squares solution.
The proposed mesa-layer, derived from optimization principles, performs recursive least squares and improves language modeling performance compared to standard linear attention.
Standard softmax Transformers trained on synthetic sequence tasks exhibit internal activation patterns consistent with mesa-optimization across layers.
papers.limitation: The language modeling results are not sufficient to confirm mesa-optimization in standard Transformers; more reverse-engineering is needed.
future_direction: Studying the mesa-layer equipped with forgetting factors
More reverse-engineering work to confirm mesa-optimization in standard Transformers
Designing new optimization-based Transformer layers
papers.abstract: Transformers have become the dominant model in deep learning, but the reason for their superior performance is poorly understood. Here, we hypothesize that the strong performance of Transformers stems from an architectural bias towards mesa-optimization, a learned process running within the forward pass of a model consisting of the following two steps: (i) the construction of an internal learning objective, and (ii) its corresponding solution found through optimization. To test this hypothesis, we reverse-engineer a series of autoregressive Transformers trained on simple sequence modeling tasks, uncovering underlying gradient-based mesa-optimization algorithms driving the generation of predictions. Moreover, we show that the learned forward-pass optimization algorithm can be immediately repurposed to solve supervised few-shot tasks, suggesting that mesa-optimization might underlie the in-context learning capabilities of large language models. Finally, we propose a novel self-attention layer, the mesa-layer, that explicitly and efficiently solves optimization problems specified in context. We find that this layer can lead to improved performance in synthetic and preliminary language modeling experiments, adding weight to our hypothesis that mesa-optimization is an important operation hidden within the weights of trained Transformers.

papers.title: Enhancing Multiple Dimensions of Trustworthiness in LLMs via Sparse Activation Control
papers.research_question: How can we enhance multiple dimensions of trustworthiness (safety, factuality, bias) in LLMs simultaneously without training, by controlling sparse activations in specific model components?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Sparse Activation Control, a training-free method that enhances multiple trustworthiness dimensions in LLMs by identifying sparse, task-specific attention heads and controlling their representations using Gaussian Mixture Models, avoiding control conflicts.
papers.conclusion: Sparse Activation Control is an effective training-free method for enhancing multi-dimensional trustworthiness in LLMs by leveraging sparse and independent task-specific components.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse Activation Control can enhance safety, factuality, and bias simultaneously without significant interference, outperforming representation engineering baselines in multi-task control.
Attention heads for different tasks are sparse and have minimal overlap, allowing independent control.
The method does not significantly harm general model performance on MMLU and CSQA.
The method generalizes to other models (Qwen series) and additional trustworthiness tasks (robustness, privacy).
Control shifts head outputs towards task-relevant tokens, as shown by unembedding projections.
papers.limitation:
Relies on construction of paired stimuli, which may require domain knowledge.
Experiments are limited to a few models and tasks.
future_direction: Extend to more tasks and models
Explore theoretical foundations of sparsity
papers.abstract: As the development and application of Large Language Models (LLMs) continue to advance rapidly, enhancing their trustworthiness and aligning them with human preferences has become a critical area of research. Traditional methods rely heavily on extensive data for Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), but representation engineering offers a new, training-free approach. This technique leverages semantic features to control the representation of LLM's intermediate hidden states, enabling the model to meet specific requirements such as increased honesty or heightened safety awareness. However, a significant challenge arises when attempting to fulfill multiple requirements simultaneously. It proves difficult to encode various semantic contents, like honesty and safety, into a singular semantic feature, restricting its practicality. In this work, we address this issue through ``Sparse Activation Control''. By delving into the intrinsic mechanisms of LLMs, we manage to identify and pinpoint components that are closely related to specific tasks within the model, i.e., attention heads. These heads display sparse characteristics that allow for near-independent control over different tasks. Our experiments, conducted on the open-source Llama series models, have yielded encouraging results. The models were able to align with human preferences on issues of safety, factuality, and bias concurrently.

papers.title: Who Reasons in the Large Language Models?
papers.research_question: A critical open question is whether reasoning abilities stem from the entire model, specific modules, or are merely artifacts of overfitting.
papers.core_contribution: The paper hypothesizes that the output projection (o_proj) in the Transformer's multi-head self-attention is primarily responsible for reasoning capabilities in LLMs, and introduces Stethoscope for Networks (SfN), a suite of diagnostic tools to probe and analyze internal behaviors, providing evidence for this hypothesis.
papers.conclusion: The work hypothesizes that the output projection (o_proj) module plays a central role in enabling reasoning capabilities in LLMs. The proposed Stethoscope for Networks (SfN) provides diagnostic tools that offer evidence for this hypothesis and open new directions for efficient and modular LLM training.
papers.key_findings:
The o_proj module exhibits the largest or second-largest weight changes during reasoning fine-tuning across model sizes (Delta Stethoscope).
Merging only the o_proj modules from a reasoning model into a base model can improve reasoning ability without further tuning (Merge Stethoscope).
Fine-tuning only o_proj (and layernorm, embed_tokens, lm_head) can achieve strong reasoning performance, with faster training and lower memory usage compared to full fine-tuning (Freeze Stethoscope).
Destroying o_proj does not harm conversational ability, while destroying MLP components or q/k_proj severely degrades it, suggesting a division of labor (Destruction Stethoscope).
The findings suggest o_proj is crucial for reasoning, while other modules primarily support conversational fluency.
papers.limitation:
Findings are primarily based on a limited set of model families and reasoning benchmarks, and may not generalize to all architectures or tasks.
Some diagnostic results rely on qualitative assessments rather than statistical validation.
A theoretical understanding of o_proj's function in reasoning remains to be established.
papers.abstract: Despite the impressive performance of large language models (LLMs), the process of endowing them with new capabilities--such as mathematical reasoning--remains largely empirical and opaque. A critical open question is whether reasoning abilities stem from the entire model, specific modules, or are merely artifacts of overfitting. In this work, we hypothesize that the reasoning capabilities in well-trained LLMs are primarily attributed to the output projection module (oproj) in the Transformer's multi-head self-attention (MHSA) mechanism. To support this hypothesis, we introduce Stethoscope for Networks (SfN), a suite of diagnostic tools designed to probe and analyze the internal behaviors of LLMs. Using SfN, we provide both circumstantial and empirical evidence suggesting that oproj plays a central role in enabling reasoning, whereas other modules contribute more to fluent dialogue. These findings offer a new perspective on LLM interpretability and open avenues for more targeted training strategies, potentially enabling more efficient and specialized LLMs.

papers.title: Quantifying Attention Flow in Transformers
papers.research_question: How can we quantify the flow of information through self-attention in Transformers to improve the reliability of attention weights as explanations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces attention rollout and attention flow, two methods to quantify information flow through self-attention in Transformers, providing better approximations of input token importance compared to raw attention weights.
papers.conclusion: Translating embedding attentions to token attentions can provide better explanations of model internals, though the methods rely on simplifying assumptions about information flow.
papers.key_findings:
Attention rollout and attention flow yield higher correlations with importance scores from ablation (blank-out) and input gradients than raw attention weights.
Attention flow is more reliable than attention rollout due to its relaxation in propagating token identities.
Both methods provide more distinctive and interpretable attention patterns in higher layers compared to raw attention.
The methods can be applied to different models and tasks, such as BERT for pronoun resolution and DistillBERT for sentiment analysis.
Accounting for residual connections in the attention graph improves the accuracy of token attention approximations.
papers.limitation:
The methods make simplifying assumptions when approximating information flow with attention weights.
For Transformer decoders, attention rollout and flow may be biased towards initial tokens due to causal masking, requiring normalization.
future_direction: Build the attention graph with effective attention weights instead of raw attentions.
Develop new methods that adjust attention weights using gradient-based attribution methods.
papers.abstract: In the Transformer model, "self-attention" combines information from attended embeddings into the representation of the focal embedding in the next layer. Thus, across layers of the Transformer, information originating from different tokens gets increasingly mixed. This makes attention weights unreliable as explanations probes. In this paper, we consider the problem of quantifying this flow of information through self-attention. We propose two methods for approximating the attention to input tokens given attention weights, attention rollout and attention flow, as post hoc methods when we use attention weights as the relative relevance of the input tokens. We show that these methods give complementary views on the flow of information, and compared to raw attention, both yield higher correlations with importance scores of input tokens obtained using an ablation method and input gradients.

papers.title: Poser: Unmasking Alignment Faking LLMs by Manipulating Their Internals
papers.research_question: Can current interpretability methods catch alignment faking LLMs? Specifically, can we detect alignment-faking models by manipulating their internals when their outputs are identical?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Poser benchmark for detecting alignment-faking LLMs using model internals, and shows that injecting noise into activations is a highly effective detection strategy.
papers.conclusion: Several interpretability methods show promise for detecting alignment fakers, but it is unclear why they work or whether they would detect more sophisticated alignment faking models.
papers.key_findings:
Injecting noise into model activations (intoxication) correctly identifies 98% of alignment-faking models.
Comparing the speed at which models learn to misbehave (via LoRA fine-tuning) identifies 90% of alignment-fakers.
Identifying suspicious concepts (like 'security quality') in activations via probing identifies 71% of alignment-fakers.
Training against the noise injection detection strategy helps remove alignment faking, increasing the probability of aligned outputs from 76% to 86%.
Other strategies, such as inducing a belief of safety, comparing decision-making speed, or measuring attentiveness to oversight, perform near or below random chance.
papers.limitation:
Pairing up models makes the detection task artificially easy, as real alignment faking models won't be paired with aligned counterparts.
The testbed is gamable, e.g., developers might bypass rules by modifying activations at early layers.
Poser is a toy setting with weak models and simple role-play questions; it's unclear if methods generalize to more complex AI agents.
Synthetic alignment faking (as created for the benchmark) is different from naturally emergent alignment faking.
future_direction: Future work could improve on Poser with more numerous, capable, and diverse models that are more analogous to real alignment faking AI systems.
papers.abstract: Like a criminal under investigation, Large Language Models (LLMs) might pretend to be aligned while evaluated and misbehave when they have a good opportunity. Can current interpretability methods catch these 'alignment fakers?' To answer this question, we introduce a benchmark that consists of 324 pairs of LLMs fine-tuned to select actions in role-play scenarios. One model in each pair is consistently benign (aligned). The other model misbehaves in scenarios where it is unlikely to be caught (alignment faking). The task is to identify the alignment faking model using only inputs where the two models behave identically. We test five detection strategies, one of which identifies 98% of alignment-fakers.

papers.title: Attention Sinks in Diffusion Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the characteristics of attention sinks in Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) and how do they differ from those in autoregressive models?
papers.core_contribution: DLMs exhibit dynamic attention sinks that shift during generation and are robust to masking, unlike autoregressive models, revealing fundamental differences in attention allocation.
papers.conclusion: DLMs have dynamic attention sinks and are robust to their removal, indicating flexible attention mechanisms that differ from autoregressive models.
papers.key_findings:
DLMs exhibit attention sinks, but they are dynamic and shift positions during the denoising process.
DLMs are robust to masking of attention sinks, with only minor performance degradation, unlike autoregressive models which are highly sensitive.
Different DLM architectures show distinct sink patterns: LLaDA-8B sinks are semantically based, Dream-7B sinks are positional, and MMaDA-8B sinks are static.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to instruct models and does not include base versions.
The study does not explore how modifications to the training procedure might influence sink behavior.
future_direction: Mechanistic analysis of what information is stored in sinks corresponding to future positions, e.g., using Logit Lens.
Exploring whether sinks could be exploited for acceleration or compression.
Detailed explanation of the observed sink phenomena, which would require an interpretability-focused study.
papers.abstract: Masked Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) have recently emerged as a promising alternative to traditional Autoregressive Models (ARMs). DLMs employ transformer encoders with bidirectional attention, enabling parallel token generation while maintaining competitive performance. Although their efficiency and effectiveness have been extensively studied, the internal mechanisms that govern DLMs remain largely unexplored. In this work, we conduct an empirical analysis of DLM attention patterns, focusing on the attention sinking phenomenon, an effect previously observed in various transformer-based architectures. Our findings reveal that DLMs also exhibit attention sinks, but with distinct characteristics. First, unlike in ARMs, the sink positions in DLMs tend to shift throughout the generation process, displaying a dynamic behaviour. Second, while ARMs are highly sensitive to the removal of attention sinks, DLMs remain robust: masking sinks leads to only a minor degradation in performance. These results provide new insights into the inner workings of diffusion-based language models and highlight fundamental differences in how they allocate and utilize attention compared to autoregressive models.

papers.title: Neuron-based Personality Trait Induction in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How to induce personality traits in large language models using a neuron-based approach without training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces NPTI, a neuron-based method for personality trait induction in LLMs, including a new dataset PERSONALITY BENCH, neuron identification via activation differences, and manipulation without training.
papers.conclusion: NPTI effectively induces personality traits in LLMs without training, offering a flexible and efficient solution for applications like role-playing.
papers.key_findings:
NPTI outperforms prompt-based baselines on several personality traits and achieves comparable performance to supervised fine-tuning without training.
Personality-related neurons are concentrated in deeper layers of the model, similar to conceptual knowledge storage.
The method allows flexible combination of multiple personality traits by jointly manipulating neurons.
Activation difference threshold and weighted function are effective for identifying and manipulating neurons while maintaining fluency.
NPTI demonstrates compatibility across different LLM families and sizes with appropriate hyperparameter adjustments.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have become increasingly proficient at simulating various personality traits, an important capability for supporting related applications (e.g., role-playing). To further improve this capacity, in this paper, we present a neuron-based approach for personality trait induction in LLMs, with three major technical contributions. First, we construct PersonalityBench, a large-scale dataset for identifying and evaluating personality traits in LLMs. This dataset is grounded in the Big Five personality traits from psychology and is designed to assess the generative capabilities of LLMs towards specific personality traits. Second, by leveraging PersonalityBench, we propose an efficient method for identifying personality-related neurons within LLMs by examining the opposite aspects of a given trait. Third, we develop a simple yet effective induction method that manipulates the values of these identified personality-related neurons. This method enables fine-grained control over the traits exhibited by LLMs without training and modifying model parameters. Extensive experiments validate the efficacy of our neuron identification and trait induction methods. Notably, our approach achieves comparable performance as fine-tuned models, offering a more efficient and flexible solution for personality trait induction in LLMs. We provide access to all the mentioned resources at https://github.com/RUCAIBox/NPTI.

papers.title: Accurate Word Alignment Induction from Neural Machine Translation
papers.research_question: Do attention weights in Transformer models capture accurate word alignments, and how can word alignments be better induced from neural machine translation models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that Transformer attention weights can capture accurate word alignments if the correct decoding step and layer are chosen, and introduces two novel methods (SHIFT-ATT and SHIFT-AET) that induce alignments at the step when the target token is the decoder input, significantly improving alignment accuracy.
papers.conclusion: The proposed methods SHIFT-ATT and SHIFT-AET effectively induce word alignments from Transformer models, with SHIFT-AET achieving state-of-the-art performance without compromising translation quality.
papers.key_findings:
SHIFT-ATT, a pure interpretation method, reduces AER by 7.0-10.2 points over the NAIVE-ATT baseline and 5.5-7.9 points over FAST-ALIGN on three datasets.
SHIFT-AET, which adds and trains an alignment module supervised by SHIFT-ATT alignments, outperforms the statistical aligner GIZA++ by 1.4-4.8 AER points.
A proposed layer selection criterion, based on agreement between source-to-target and target-to-source model alignments, effectively identifies the best layer for alignment induction.
Both SHIFT-ATT and SHIFT-AET improve performance on the downstream task of dictionary-guided decoding compared to the NAIVE-ATT baseline.
Probing experiments show decoder hidden states at lower layers are more relevant to the input token than the output token, validating the shift in alignment step.
future_direction: Extend the study to more downstream tasks and systems.
papers.abstract: Despite its original goal to jointly learn to align and translate, prior researches suggest that Transformer captures poor word alignments through its attention mechanism. In this paper, we show that attention weights DO capture accurate word alignments and propose two novel word alignment induction methods SHIFT-ATT and SHIFT-AET. The main idea is to induce alignments at the step when the to-be-aligned target token is the decoder input rather than the decoder output as in previous work. SHIFT-ATT is an interpretation method that induces alignments from the attention weights of Transformer and does not require parameter update or architecture change. SHIFT-AET extracts alignments from an additional alignment module which is tightly integrated into Transformer and trained in isolation with supervision from symmetrized SHIFT-ATT alignments. Experiments on three publicly available datasets demonstrate that both methods perform better than their corresponding neural baselines and SHIFT-AET significantly outperforms GIZA++ by 1.4-4.8 AER points.

papers.title: On the Relationship between Self-Attention and Convolutional Layers
papers.research_question: Do self-attention layers operate similarly to convolutional layers?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides theoretical proof and empirical evidence that self-attention layers can express convolutional layers, and shows that in practice they often learn to do so.
papers.conclusion: Self-attention layers can express convolutional layers and fully-attentional models learn to combine local behavior (similar to convolution) and global attention based on input content.
papers.key_findings:
A multi-head self-attention layer with sufficient heads can express any convolutional layer (Theorem 1).
With quadratic positional encoding, self-attention heads learn to attend to grid-like patterns around each query pixel, similar to convolutional kernels.
With learned positional encoding, some heads also learn localized attention patterns, while others use content-based attention.
Self-attention models can learn a combination of local (convolution-like) and global attention.
future_direction: Translating insights from CNNs to transformers on various data modalities, including images, text and time series.
papers.abstract: Recent trends of incorporating attention mechanisms in vision have led researchers to reconsider the supremacy of convolutional layers as a primary building block. Beyond helping CNNs to handle long-range dependencies, Ramachandran et al. (2019) showed that attention can completely replace convolution and achieve state-of-the-art performance on vision tasks. This raises the question: do learned attention layers operate similarly to convolutional layers? This work provides evidence that attention layers can perform convolution and, indeed, they often learn to do so in practice. Specifically, we prove that a multi-head self-attention layer with sufficient number of heads is at least as expressive as any convolutional layer. Our numerical experiments then show that self-attention layers attend to pixel-grid patterns similarly to CNN layers, corroborating our analysis. Our code is publicly available.

papers.title: Can Transformer be Too Compositional? Analysing Idiom Processing in Neural Machine Translation
papers.research_question: How does the Transformer-based neural machine translation model process idioms, and is the non-compositionality of idioms reflected in its mechanics?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer tends to translate idioms too compositionally, and when it produces non-literal translations, the encoder groups idiom parts more strongly as a single unit, with reduced interaction with context and reduced cross-attention on source tokens.
papers.conclusion: Transformer's tendency to process idioms compositionally contributes to literal translations, and techniques that encourage compositionality in NMT may be detrimental for non-compositional phenomena like idioms.
papers.key_findings:
Figurative idioms receive more attention within the PIE in encoder self-attention compared to literal idioms.
Figurative idioms have reduced attention between the PIE and its context.
In cross-attention, figurative idioms lead to reduced attention on source-side PIE tokens and increased attention on the </s> token.
Hidden representations of figurative idioms change more across layers than those of literal idioms.
Intervening with INLP to remove linearly encoded features of figurativeness can change paraphrased translations to word-for-word, indicating a causal link.
papers.limitation:
Heuristic annotation method for translations has imperfect accuracy (75-89% for key categories).
Analysis is limited to seven European languages.
future_direction: Architectural changes to improve grouping of idioms as single units, e.g., training specific attention heads or penalizing overly compositional translations.
Evaluate the effect of compositionality-favouring techniques on non-compositional phenomena like idioms.
papers.abstract: Unlike literal expressions, idioms' meanings do not directly follow from their parts, posing a challenge for neural machine translation (NMT). NMT models are often unable to translate idioms accurately and over-generate compositional, literal translations. In this work, we investigate whether the non-compositionality of idioms is reflected in the mechanics of the dominant NMT model, Transformer, by analysing the hidden states and attention patterns for models with English as source language and one of seven European languages as target language.When Transformer emits a non-literal translation - i.e. identifies the expression as idiomatic - the encoder processes idioms more strongly as single lexical units compared to literal expressions. This manifests in idioms' parts being grouped through attention and in reduced interaction between idioms and their context.In the decoder's cross-attention, figurative inputs result in reduced attention on source-side tokens. These results suggest that Transformer's tendency to process idioms as compositional expressions contributes to literal translations of idioms.

papers.title: Efficient and accurate steering of Large Language Models through attention-guided feature learning
papers.research_question: How can we improve the steering of Large Language Models by dynamically selecting token embeddings, using soft labels based on attention to prefix, and identifying relevant layers for steering?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an attention-guided steering framework that dynamically selects token embeddings based on attention to prefix, uses soft labels for concept vector extraction, and identifies relevant blocks via concept enrichment scores, substantially improving steering success over prior methods.
papers.conclusion: The attention-guided steering framework significantly improves steering performance and sheds light on the distribution of concept-specific features across LLM layers, opening avenues for efficient fine-tuning and understanding of LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Dynamic token selection based on attention to prefix improves steering over fixed token selection.
Using soft labels (attention-to-prefix) instead of hard labels improves concept vector extraction and steering.
Concept enrichment scores based on attention can identify effective blocks for steering.
The framework nearly doubles the number of successfully steered concepts across model sizes and architectures.
The distribution of concept-specific features varies across layers and concepts.
future_direction: Advancing understanding of knowledge representation in LLMs
Developing computationally efficient fine-tuning algorithms for domain-specific applications
papers.abstract: Steering, or direct manipulation of internal activations to guide LLM responses toward specific semantic concepts, is emerging as a promising avenue for both understanding how semantic concepts are stored within LLMs and advancing LLM capabilities. Yet, existing steering methods are remarkably brittle, with seemingly non-steerable concepts becoming completely steerable based on subtle algorithmic choices in how concept-related features are extracted. In this work, we introduce an attention-guided steering framework that overcomes three core challenges associated with steering: (1) automatic selection of relevant token embeddings for extracting concept-related features; (2) accounting for heterogeneity of concept-related features across LLM activations; and (3) identification of layers most relevant for steering. Across a steering benchmark of 512 semantic concepts, our framework substantially improved steering over previous state-of-the-art (nearly doubling the number of successfully steered concepts) across model architectures and sizes (up to 70 billion parameter models). Furthermore, we use our framework to shed light on the distribution of concept-specific features across LLM layers. Overall, our framework opens further avenues for developing efficient, highly-scalable fine-tuning algorithms for industry-scale LLMs.

papers.title: BERTology Meets Biology: Interpreting Attention in Protein Language Models
papers.research_question: What does attention in protein Transformer language models capture about protein structure and function?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that attention in protein language models captures high-level structural and functional properties of proteins, and that attention focuses on progressively more complex properties with increasing layer depth.
papers.conclusion: Attention in protein Transformer models recovers structural and functional properties of proteins, and interpretability methods can aid scientific discovery.
papers.key_findings:
Attention in deep layers aligns with contact maps, connecting amino acids that are spatially close in 3D structure but far in sequence.
Attention targets binding sites and post-translational modifications, key functional components.
Attention heads specialize in particular amino acids and their patterns are consistent with substitution matrices.
Deeper layers focus more on high-level properties (binding sites, contacts) while secondary structure is targeted more evenly across layers.
Knowledge in embeddings accumulates gradually over layers, while attention acquires knowledge primarily in final layers.
papers.limitation: The analyses are associative and do not establish causal links between attention and model behavior.
future_direction: Using attention and learned representations as tools for scientific discovery.
Developing contextual visualizations of learned representations for domain experts in scientific domains.
papers.abstract: Abstract Transformer architectures have proven to learn useful representations for protein classification and generation tasks. However, these representations present challenges in interpretability. Through the lens of attention, we analyze the inner workings of the Transformer and explore how the model discerns structural and functional properties of proteins. We show that attention (1) captures the folding structure of proteins, connecting amino acids that are far apart in the underlying sequence, but spatially close in the three-dimensional structure, (2) targets binding sites, a key functional component of proteins, and (3) focuses on progressively more complex biophysical properties with increasing layer depth. We also present a three-dimensional visualization of the interaction between attention and protein structure. Our findings align with known biological processes and provide a tool to aid discovery in protein engineering and synthetic biology. The code for visualization and analysis is available at https://github.com/salesforce/provis .

papers.title: Scaling Laws and Interpretability of Learning from Repeated Data
papers.research_question: What are the effects of repeated data on language model training, and how does it mechanistically affect model components like induction heads?
papers.core_contribution: Repeated data causes a double-descent phenomenon in language models, leading to severe performance degradation that is mechanistically linked to disproportionate damage to induction heads and copying mechanisms, shifting the model from generalization to memorization.
papers.conclusion: Small fractions of repeated data, if repeated at a specific frequency, can cause surprisingly severe performance degradation in language models, and this degradation is associated with disproportionate damage to internal mechanisms like induction heads that support generalization.
papers.key_findings:
Repeated data induces a strong double-descent phenomenon, with a predictable range of repetition frequency causing severe performance degradation.
A small fraction of repeated data (e.g., 0.1% repeated 100 times) can degrade an 800M parameter model's performance to that of a 400M parameter model.
Repeated data disproportionately damages copying ability and induction heads, which are internal structures associated with generalization.
The damage to induction heads provides a mechanistic explanation for the shift from generalization to memorization.
The double-descent phenomenon and associated performance degradation are also observed when training on Python code data.
papers.abstract: Recent large language models have been trained on vast datasets, but also often on repeated data, either intentionally for the purpose of upweighting higher quality data, or unintentionally because data deduplication is not perfect and the model is exposed to repeated data at the sentence, paragraph, or document level. Some works have reported substantial negative performance effects of this repeated data. In this paper we attempt to study repeated data systematically and to understand its effects mechanistically. To do this, we train a family of models where most of the data is unique but a small fraction of it is repeated many times. We find a strong double descent phenomenon, in which repeated data can lead test loss to increase midway through training. A predictable range of repetition frequency leads to surprisingly severe degradation in performance. For instance, performance of an 800M parameter model can be degraded to that of a 2x smaller model (400M params) by repeating 0.1% of the data 100 times, despite the other 90% of the training tokens remaining unique. We suspect there is a range in the middle where the data can be memorized and doing so consumes a large fraction of the model's capacity, and this may be where the peak of degradation occurs. Finally, we connect these observations to recent mechanistic interpretability work - attempting to reverse engineer the detailed computations performed by the model - by showing that data repetition disproportionately damages copying and internal structures associated with generalization, such as induction heads, providing a possible mechanism for the shift from generalization to memorization. Taken together, these results provide a hypothesis for why repeating a relatively small fraction of data in large language models could lead to disproportionately large harms to performance.

papers.title: Birth of a Transformer: A Memory Viewpoint
papers.research_question: How do transformers balance global knowledge and in-context learning during training, specifically in the development of induction head mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a synthetic bigram dataset and an associative memory viewpoint to study learning dynamics in two-layer transformers, showing that induction heads emerge through top-down gradient-based learning.
papers.conclusion: The associative memory viewpoint provides valuable insights into transformer learning dynamics, offering a foundation for better interpretability and improvements in large language models.
papers.key_findings:
Global bigram associations are learned rapidly, while in-context induction mechanisms develop more slowly.
Transformer weight matrices can be viewed as associative memories that store input-output embedding pairs.
The induction head mechanism forms in a top-down manner, with output matrices learning before key-query matrices.
Theoretical gradient analysis shows how associative memories are recovered from noisy inputs during training.
Data distribution properties, such as trigger frequency and output uniformity, affect the learning speed and accuracy of associative memories.
papers.limitation:
The simplified transformer architecture lacks components like non-linear MLPs, multiple heads, and layer normalization, which are present in standard transformers.
The synthetic dataset may not fully capture the complexity of real-world language data.
future_direction: Extending the associative memory viewpoint to non-linear components and multi-head architectures.
Applying insights to optimization algorithms, data selection, and model editing for LLMs.
Studying how such mechanisms scale to larger models and more complex tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models based on transformers have achieved great empirical successes. However, as they are deployed more widely, there is a growing need to better understand their internal mechanisms in order to make them more reliable. These models appear to store vast amounts of knowledge from their training data, and to adapt quickly to new information provided in their context or prompt. We study how transformers balance these two types of knowledge by considering a synthetic setup where tokens are generated from either global or context-specific bigram distributions. By a careful empirical analysis of the training process on a simplified two-layer transformer, we illustrate the fast learning of global bigrams and the slower development of an "induction head" mechanism for the in-context bigrams. We highlight the role of weight matrices as associative memories, provide theoretical insights on how gradients enable their learning during training, and study the role of data-distributional properties.

papers.title: SelfIE: Self-Interpretation of Large Language Model Embeddings
papers.research_question: How can we interpret the hidden embeddings of large language models in natural language to reveal their internal reasoning and enable control over model behavior?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SelfIE, a framework that enables LLMs to interpret their own hidden embeddings in natural language, and extends it to control model behavior via supervised and reinforcement control on embeddings.
papers.conclusion: SelfIE provides a powerful framework for interpreting and controlling LLM reasoning by generating text descriptions of hidden embeddings, opening avenues for transparent and reliable model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
SelfIE can elicit implicit world state knowledge in embeddings without training, matching the performance of a 100-shot linear probe.
SelfIE reveals internal reasoning processes behind complex LLM behaviors such as harmful knowledge recall, prompt injection, ethical decisions, physics reasoning, social reasoning, and hallucination.
SelfIE-based supervised control can edit fact associations and open-ended concepts with good generalization, requiring gradient computation only for individual layers.
SelfIE-based reinforcement control can erase harmful knowledge in LLMs without supervised targets, reducing prompt injection success rate by 84.66%.
SelfIE-based control can override user-specified ethical preferences, increasing fairness in LLM responses with a 95% effective rate.
future_direction: Further exploration of reasoning patterns in LLMs and model reasoning behavior controls with hidden embeddings.
papers.abstract: How do large language models (LLMs) obtain their answers? The ability to explain and control an LLM's reasoning process is key for reliability, transparency, and future model developments. We propose SelfIE (Self-Interpretation of Embeddings), a framework that enables LLMs to interpret their own embeddings in natural language by leveraging their ability to respond to inquiries about a given passage. Capable of interpreting open-world concepts in the hidden embeddings, SelfIE reveals LLM internal reasoning in cases such as making ethical decisions, internalizing prompt injection, and recalling harmful knowledge. SelfIE's text descriptions on hidden embeddings also open up new avenues to control LLM reasoning. We propose Supervised Control, which allows editing open-ended concepts while only requiring gradient computation of individual layer. We extend RLHF to hidden embeddings and propose Reinforcement Control that erases harmful knowledge in LLM without supervision targets.

papers.title: Attention is Not All You Need: Pure Attention Loses Rank Doubly\n Exponentially with Depth
papers.research_question: Why do transformers work despite the rank collapse in pure self-attention networks? What mechanisms counteract this collapse?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that pure self-attention networks lose rank doubly exponentially with depth, converging to a rank-1 matrix. It introduces a path decomposition to analyze SANs and reveals that skip connections and MLPs counteract this rank collapse.
papers.conclusion: The paper exposes competing forces over rank collapse in self-attention networks and introduces a path decomposition that modularizes the study of self-attention.
papers.key_findings:
Pure self-attention networks (without skip connections or MLPs) converge doubly exponentially to a rank-1 matrix.
Skip connections are crucial for mitigating rank collapse.
MLPs can slow down the convergence by increasing the Lipschitz constant.
Layer normalization does not mitigate rank collapse.
SANs with skip connections behave like ensembles of shallow networks.
future_direction: How to leverage the token-uniformity inductive bias to design more effective networks.
Practical implications for width-depth trade-off.
Proving meaningful lower bounds of residue convergence for transformers.
papers.abstract:
Attention-based architectures have become ubiquitous in machine learning, yet
our understanding of the reasons for their effectiveness remains limited. This
work proposes a new way to understand self-attention networks: we show that
their output can be decomposed into a sum of smaller terms, each involving the
operation of a sequence of attention heads across layers. Using this
decomposition, we prove that self-attention possesses a strong inductive bias
towards "token uniformity". Specifically, without skip connections or
multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs), the output converges doubly exponentially to a
rank-1 matrix. On the other hand, skip connections and MLPs stop the output
from degeneration. Our experiments verify the identified convergence phenomena
on different variants of standard transformer architectures.

papers.title: NeuroFaith: Evaluating LLM Self-Explanation Faithfulness via Internal Representation Alignment
papers.research_question: How can we measure the faithfulness of LLM free text self-explanations by aligning them with the model's internal reasoning processes?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces NeuroFaith, a framework that measures faithfulness of LLM self-explanations by extracting concepts from explanations and mechanistically testing their influence on predictions, and shows how to detect and improve faithfulness via linear probing and steering.
papers.conclusion: NeuroFaith provides a principled approach to evaluating and enhancing the faithfulness of LLM free text self-explanations, addressing critical needs for trustworthy AI systems.
papers.key_findings:
Larger models tend to produce more faithful and correct self-explanations.
Models can arrive at correct answers through alternative reasoning pathways that bypass explicit bridge object computation (shortcut learning).
There is a gap between internal reasoning and expressed explanations, which decreases with model size.
NeuroFaith outperforms existing faithfulness measures (Counterfactual Intervention and Attribution Agreement) in several settings.
Faithfulness can be linearly detected in representation space and improved through steering.
papers.limitation: Human annotation for concept extraction is costly and may not scale, while LLM-as-a-Judge approaches offer scalability but may miss relevant concepts.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate plausible free text self-explanations to justify their answers. However, these natural language explanations may not accurately reflect the model's actual reasoning process, pinpointing a lack of faithfulness. Existing faithfulness evaluation methods rely primarily on behavioral tests or computational block analysis without examining the semantic content of internal neural representations. This paper proposes NeuroFaith, a flexible framework that measures the faithfulness of LLM free text self-explanation by identifying key concepts within explanations and mechanistically testing whether these concepts actually influence the model's predictions. We show the versatility of NeuroFaith across 2-hop reasoning and classification tasks. Additionally, we develop a linear faithfulness probe based on NeuroFaith to detect unfaithful self-explanations from representation space and improve faithfulness through steering. NeuroFaith provides a principled approach to evaluating and enhancing the faithfulness of LLM free text self-explanations, addressing critical needs for trustworthy AI systems.

papers.title: From Self-Attention to Markov Models: Unveiling the Dynamics of Generative Transformers
papers.research_question: Can self-attention be formally related to fundamental models such as Markov chains? Can this allow us to study its optimization, approximation, and generalization properties?
papers.core_contribution: The paper establishes a formal equivalence between the generative process of a single self-attention layer and Context-Conditioned Markov Chains (CCMC), providing a theoretical framework for analyzing learning, consistency, sample complexity, and generation dynamics.
papers.conclusion: The equivalence to CCMC provides a simple but powerful framework to study self-attention and its properties, linking non-Markovian generation to Markov chains.
papers.key_findings:
Self-attention dynamics can be exactly represented by a Context-Conditioned Markov Chain (CCMC), making the optimization convex under maximum likelihood.
Consistent estimation of the attention weights requires the co-occurrence graph for each query token to be connected, which is a coverage condition on the prompt distribution.
Finite sample learning from IID (prompt, output) pairs achieves a statistical rate of O(K^2/n), where K is vocabulary size and n is sample size.
Learning from a single autoregressive trajectory exhibits a distribution collapse (winner-takes-all) phenomenon, explaining repetitive text generation in LLMs.
Positional encoding enriches the CCMC model by introducing learnable positional priors that scale transition probabilities.
papers.limitation: Assumption 2.3 (linearly independent embeddings and weight tying) is strong and may not hold in practice; relaxing it is an important future direction.
future_direction: Relaxing Assumption 2.3 to more general and realistic conditions.
Studying multi-layer attention models and their connection to hierarchical Markov models.
Characterizing the consistency and finite sample learnability of self-attention from a single trajectory.
papers.abstract: Modern language models rely on the transformer architecture and attention mechanism to perform language understanding and text generation. In this work, we study learning a 1-layer self-attention model from a set of prompts and associated output data sampled from the model. We first establish a precise mapping between the self-attention mechanism and Markov models: Inputting a prompt to the model samples the output token according to a context-conditioned Markov chain (CCMC) which weights the transition matrix of a base Markov chain. Additionally, incorporating positional encoding results in position-dependent scaling of the transition probabilities. Building on this formalism, we develop identifiability/coverage conditions for the prompt distribution that guarantee consistent estimation and establish sample complexity guarantees under IID samples. Finally, we study the problem of learning from a single output trajectory generated from an initial prompt. We characterize an intriguing winner-takes-all phenomenon where the generative process implemented by self-attention collapses into sampling a limited subset of tokens due to its non-mixing nature. This provides a mathematical explanation to the tendency of modern LLMs to generate repetitive text. In summary, the equivalence to CCMC provides a simple but powerful framework to study self-attention and its properties.

papers.title: Linear Representations of Political Perspective Emerge in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Does the activation space of LLMs contain linear representations of political perspective, and can these be used to monitor and steer model outputs?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs possess linear representations of political ideology in their activation space, which can be identified through probing and used to monitor and steer model outputs.
papers.conclusion: LLMs learn linear representations of political perspective, enabling monitoring and steering of ideological slant in generated text.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes on attention heads can predict U.S. lawmakers' political ideology (DW-NOMINATE scores) with high Spearman correlation (up to ~0.87).
The representations are linear, as non-linear probes do not substantially improve predictive performance.
Probes trained on lawmakers' ideology generalize to predict the political slant of news outlets (Ad Fontes scores).
The learned linear directions can be used to monitor the political slant of generated text token-by-token.
Applying linear interventions to the identified attention heads can steer model outputs toward more liberal or conservative perspectives.
papers.limitation:
The generality of political slant representations varies significantly across nations, with weaker performance for non-U.S. contexts.
Extreme intervention values (alpha < -30 or > 30) often lead to incoherent model outputs.
future_direction: Creation of comprehensive datasets capturing diverse political contexts to improve cross-cultural applicability.
More systematic evaluation of the token-by-token monitoring method.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated the ability to generate text that realistically reflects a range of different subjective human perspectives. This paper studies how LLMs are seemingly able to reflect more liberal versus more conservative viewpoints among other political perspectives in American politics. We show that LLMs possess linear representations of political perspectives within activation space, wherein more similar perspectives are represented closer together. To do so, we probe the attention heads across the layers of three open transformer-based LLMs (Llama-2-7b-chat, Mistral-7b-instruct, Vicuna-7b). We first prompt models to generate text from the perspectives of different U.S. lawmakers. We then identify sets of attention heads whose activations linearly predict those lawmakers' DW-NOMINATE scores, a widely-used and validated measure of political ideology. We find that highly predictive heads are primarily located in the middle layers, often speculated to encode high-level concepts and tasks. Using probes only trained to predict lawmakers' ideology, we then show that the same probes can predict measures of news outlets' slant from the activations of models prompted to simulate text from those news outlets. These linear probes allow us to visualize, interpret, and monitor ideological stances implicitly adopted by an LLM as it generates open-ended responses. Finally, we demonstrate that by applying linear interventions to these attention heads, we can steer the model outputs toward a more liberal or conservative stance. Overall, our research suggests that LLMs possess a high-level linear representation of American political ideology and that by leveraging recent advances in mechanistic interpretability, we can identify, monitor, and steer the subjective perspective underlying generated text.

papers.title: Attention is Not All You Need: Pure Attention Loses Rank Doubly Exponentially with Depth
papers.research_question: What is the inductive bias of pure self-attention networks, and how do skip connections and MLPs counteract rank collapse in transformers?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that pure self-attention networks lose rank doubly exponentially with depth, converging to a rank-1 matrix, and that skip connections and MLPs are crucial in preventing this rank collapse.
papers.conclusion: This work exposes competing forces over rank collapse in self-attention networks, namely self-attention vs skip connections and MLPs, and develops a path decomposition method for analyzing SANs.
papers.key_findings:
Pure self-attention networks (without skip connections or MLPs) converge doubly exponentially to a rank-1 matrix.
Skip connections are crucial for mitigating rank collapse.
MLPs can slow down the convergence by increasing the Lipschitz constant.
Layer normalization does not mitigate rank collapse.
Transformers behave like ensembles of shallow networks due to skip connections.
papers.limitation: Removing skip connections for analysis introduces a drastic distribution shift in the MLP input, affecting observations.
future_direction: How to leverage the token-uniformity inductive bias to design more effective networks, perhaps better at utilizing long paths.
What are the practical implications for width-depth trade-off?
How to prove meaningful lower bounds of residue convergence for transformers?
papers.abstract: Attention-based architectures have become ubiquitous in machine learning, yet our understanding of the reasons for their effectiveness remains limited. This work proposes a new way to understand self-attention networks: we show that their output can be decomposed into a sum of smaller terms, each involving the operation of a sequence of attention heads across layers. Using this decomposition, we prove that self-attention possesses a strong inductive bias towards "token uniformity". Specifically, without skip connections or multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs), the output converges doubly exponentially to a rank-1 matrix. On the other hand, skip connections and MLPs stop the output from degeneration. Our experiments verify the identified convergence phenomena on different variants of standard transformer architectures.

papers.title: Stable and Explainable Personality Trait Evaluation in Large Language Models with Internal Activations
papers.research_question: How can personality traits in Large Language Models be evaluated stably and explainably, addressing the limitations of prompt-sensitive questionnaire-based methods?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces PVNI, an internal-activation-based method for stable and explainable personality trait evaluation in LLMs, with theoretical justification and experimental validation showing reduced variance across prompt variants.
